title: Dems rally behind Michigan prosecutor to champion party in crucial House race
excerpt: Primary election battles in Michigan intensify as candidate Abdul El-Sayed faces moderate challenger Haley Stevens in a high-stakes Democratic Senate race. Progressive Change Campaign Committee co-fou...
body_text:
Primary election battles in Michigan intensify as candidate Abdul El-Sayed faces moderate challenger Haley Stevens in a high-stakes Democratic Senate race. Progressive Change Campaign Committee co-founder Adam Green analyzes the ideological clash on Fox News as candidates clash over progressive policies. Host Bill Hemmer breaks down the financial dynamics of the race, showing how fundraising numbers reflect the deep division within the state's Democratic Party.

Christina Hines, a prosecutor and Democratic candidate for Congress in Michigan's 10th Congressional District, secured her party's nomination in a primary election on Tuesday evening.

Democrats will count on Hines' messaging on affordability and her story as as a special victims prosecutor to flip the district and chip away the GOP’s slim majority in the U.S. House of Representatives.

"My work was a different kind of chaos. Protecting families from predators isn't just a job for me. It's a mission. Now families like ours are getting screwed by a system that only works for the rich," Hines said in a campaign video.

SOCIALIST-BACKED MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AMERICAN POLITICS A 'DISEASE' AFTER PROFESSING LOVE FOR US

Christina Hines, candiate for congress in Michigan's 10th congressional district, poses for a photo. (Christina Hines for Congress)

In recent years, the district has leaned Republican but remains largely competitive.

Incumbent Rep. John James, R-Mich., last won re-election in 2024 in a 51.1% to 45.0% victory over Democratic challenger Carl Marlinga, a judge and former prosecutor.

The cycle before that, James beat out Marlinga by a narrow 48.8% to 48.3% win in 2022.

But now, James, who enjoyed the benefit of incumbency, announced he would vacate the seat and instead pursue a gubernatorial bid, calling it a way to secure Michigan’s prosperity to future generations.

"My family, like countless others, came to our great state for the better opportunities our manufacturing and automotive industries offered and to live the American dream," James said in a statement.

TWIN COURT RULINGS RESHAPE HOUSE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS FIGHT UPHILL REDISTRICTING BATTLE

Republican gubernatorial candidate in Michigan, Rep. John James, R-Mich., speaks during a breakfast at Fireside Grill & Patio on Aug. 3, 2026 in Novi, Michigan. James will face off against businessman Perry Johnson in the Republican primary on Tuesday August 4. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

With an open seat in play, Hines has pitched her candidacy as a way to protect the country from what she characterized as an overzealous administration and institutional corruption.

"Congress has too many millionaires but not nearly enough moms who get things done," Hines said.

In her career as a prosecutor, Hines described her work as helping victims of sexual abuse and human trafficking, according to her website. She has also prosecuted cases involving homicide, torture and hate crimes.

On her website, Hines listed priorities like reducing the cost of living by pushing back against what she identified as "price gouging" and increasing the minimum wage, investing in technical educations and protecting federal programs against cuts from the Trump administration like Social Security, Medicaid and Medicare.

TRUMP JUST EXPANDED HIS TARIFF PLAYBOOK WITH A POWERFUL TRADE WEAPON NO PRESIDENT HAS EVER USED

U.S. President Donald Trump walks to a waiting Air Force One at the Hagerstown Regional Airport on July 31, 2026 in Hagerstown, Maryland. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Her platform has attracted endorsements from fellow local figures like Marlinga, the former Democratic nominee against James and a former Macomb County Prosecutor and Circuit Court Judge. She also received an endorsement from Michael Taylor, Sterling Heights Mayor.

With the party’s nomination secured, Hines will advance to the general election on Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: 2026 Midterms State of Play: Key races unfold as Stevens, El-Sayed battle in Michigan
excerpt: Progressive candidates like Abdul El-Sayed challenge moderate Democrats in a high-stakes Michigan primary race, highlighting a deeper ideological battle within the party. Fox News hosts Sandra Smith a...
body_text:
Progressive candidates like Abdul El-Sayed challenge moderate Democrats in a high-stakes Michigan primary race, highlighting a deeper ideological battle within the party. Fox News hosts Sandra Smith and John Roberts lead a panel analysis of this key battleground state matchup. Political analysts weigh in on how these progressive challenges will shape the party's national identity ahead of the midterm elections.

The 2026 midterms kicked into high gear Tuesday as voters headed to the polls across five states, with Michigan's marquee Democratic Senate primary leading a slate of closely watched contests.

The contest between Rep. Haley Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed has become the marquee race of the night, drawing millions of dollars in outside spending and attention from top Democratic figures.

The winner will face Republican Mike Rogers in November in one of the country's most competitive Senate races and a contest that could help determine control of the chamber.

2026 MIDTERMS: PRIMARIES, KEY RACES AND ELECTION RESULTS

Rep. Haley Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed are vying for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Michigan. (Scott Olson/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

The primary has also become a proxy fight over the Democratic Party's direction.

Stevens has been backed by much of the party establishment, while El-Sayed has rallied support from progressives including Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, fueling a broader debate over the message Democrats should carry into the general election.

DEMS SELECT THEIR CANDIDATE TO FACE LONGTIME GOP LAWMAKER WHO BALKED AT VIRGINIA REDISTRICTING

The biggest primary night of the 2026 midterms unfolded Tuesday as voters cast ballots in key races across five states. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

While Michigan has dominated national attention, voters in Kansas, Missouri, Virginia and Washington also headed to the polls Tuesday in races that will shape the November battlefield

Several contests remained outstanding late Tuesday, including Michigan's 13th Congressional District Democratic primary, where Rep. Shri Thanedar held the lead as votes continued to be counted. Many races in Washington also remained unresolved because the state conducts its elections primarily by mail.

Rep. Shri Thanedar sought renomination in Michigan's 13th Congressional District Democratic primary during the Aug. 4, 2026, midterm elections. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images))

Many Washington races were not expected to be called Tuesday night because the state conducts elections almost entirely by mail and continues accepting ballots that are postmarked by Election Day.

Washington uses a top-two primary system, in which candidates from all parties appear on the same ballot and the two candidates receiving the most votes advance to the general election, regardless of party affiliation.

As vote counting continues, particularly in Washington, where mail ballots can arrive after Election Day if postmarked on time, several contests remained outstanding Tuesday night.

The results will help define the November battlefield as both parties pivot from primary fights to the general election.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Hundreds camp in Rome heatwave as Meloni government cracks down on squats
excerpt:
Spin Time provides homes, food banks and after-school clubs but the authorities have locked out residents

Hundreds of people have spent a week sleeping in tents in the Rome heat amid a standoff betwe...
body_text:
Spin Time provides homes, food banks and after-school clubs but the authorities have locked out residents

Hundreds of people have spent a week sleeping in tents in the Rome heat amid a standoff between Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government and local politicians over the future of Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance.

A minor fire last week forced the evacuation of the building, occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, and it has remained closed as the Meloni government attempts to crack down on such squatted properties.

“It’s an awful situation, made worse by this heatwave,” said Petronela Podaro, a domestic worker from Romania camped outside the building, its huge red gates locked up, in Rome’s Esquilino district.

The fire inside Spin Time Labs broke out in the early hours of 29 July in an external area and was quickly extinguished by residents before it could spread.

Police evacuated the 10-floor complex, citing the need for safety checks, forcing about 400 residents including children, elderly and disabled people on to the street.

Spin Time Labs, an initiative supported by Rome’s leftwing council and the Vatican, has long been targeted for eviction by Meloni’s government, which regards occupied buildings as dens for criminality.

The centre, which over the last decade has transformed into a space offering various social and cultural services, including a food bank, a restaurant and co-working, hit the headlines in 2019 after an aide to the late Pope Francis, Cardinal Konrad Krajewski, climbed down a manhole to restore the electricity, provoking the fury of Matteo Salvini, who was the interior minister at the time and is now deputy prime minister.

Various Italian writers, actors and film directors, including the Oscar winner Paolo Sorrentino, have appealed for the residents to be allowed back in or for alternative accommodation to be provided.

Roberto Saviano, an author and high-profile critic of Meloni’s government, visited the scene on Monday and described the centre as a “symbol of democracy” rather than a criminal act.

The building is now under two judicial seizure orders – one linked to the private owner’s long-running legal battle to regain possession and the other to the fire.

Although shutting down Spin Time is in its plans, the interior ministry has failed to carry out an eviction order first issued by a judge in 2020, two years before Meloni came to power, reportedly due to fears over the social and legal repercussions of forcing vulnerable people on to the street. Earlier this year, the ministry, led by Matteo Piantedosi, was ordered to pay €21m in damages for failing to act on the eviction order.

As Rome’s council, which along with an army of volunteers has provided camp beds, food, drink and medical assistance, scrambles for a solution, including offering to buy the building so that the community can be maintained, Spin Time’s residents are facing more time on the street.

“There are lots of children, newborns, elderly and disabled people, and those with complicated illnesses who are struggling in this heat,” said Podaro, who is unemployed. “But we are very united community, of all nationalities and backgrounds. What this government doesn’t seem to understand is that if we had a decent job and could earn money, then we wouldn’t be in this situation.”

Spin Time has provided a lifeline for hundreds of people, including Marco Perilli, an Italian construction worker who was one of the community’s first residents after becoming homeless following a divorce.

Perilli was also among the residents who put the fire out. “There was panic but we were able to extinguish it within about 20 minutes,” he said. “Firefighters made the area safe but then the police arrived and, because we were afraid, we all went outside. They locked the gates and told us we couldn’t go back inside due to the safety checks. Within a few hours, the building was seized.”

Perilli said police searched the building for drugs and weapons. “It backfired because they found nothing,” he added, while claiming “the fire was exploited as an excuse for eviction”.

“But we will continue to fight against it,” he said. “The Meloni government needs to think carefully about the real meaning of power. Power is not about attacking poor people – this government is at war against the poor.”

Benjamin Macshane, a British volunteer cook in Spin Time’s restaurant, said the initiative provided more than just shelter. “There’s co-working, there’s an after-school club, there’s migration assistance, a food bank, a barbers, an auditorium … I can’t think of anywhere else in the world that has so many different avenues for a community to grow.”

title: ‘I just want to find them’: deadly cloudbursts devastate Kashmir’s mountain communities
excerpt:
Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock

As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief step...
body_text:
Increasingly erratic weather patterns due to climate change mean people are losing homes, crops and livestock

As rain lashed the Pir Panjal mountains before dawn on 19 July, Haji Mohammad Latief stepped outside his home in Murrah, a remote mountain village in Indian-administered Kashmir. His daughter had asked him to move the family’s car to a safer place as the rain got heavier.

“I had only just parked it,” Latief recalled. “When I turned around, I saw the water coming.” Minutes later, a cloudburst sent mud, boulders and water crashing down the hillside.

Latief, 48, had spent years building the house, where five generations of his Gujjar family lived together. Within minutes, the torrent swallowed it, trapping eight family members inside. He survived only because he had stepped outside. By dawn, everything he had built lay in rubble.

When the Guardian reached Murrah four days later, electricity, roads and mobile networks were cut off. Floodwaters had washed away roads and footbridges, leaving the only way into the village a 90-minute walk through rain and landslide debris. Residents carried sacks of flour, cooking gas cylinders and medicines across the broken crossing.

Murrah is perched high in the Pir Panjal range above the town of Bafliaz, in Poonch district, about 125 miles (200km) south-west of Srinagar, Kashmir’s main city. The village is home to mostly Gujjars, one of the largest pastoralist communities in the Himalayas, whose livelihoods have long depended on livestock, farming and seasonal migration through the mountains.

The hillside remained too unstable for excavators to reach. Soldiers, disaster response teams and local volunteers searched the debris by hand while others combed the swollen Suran River for the missing.

Latief now lives in the house of his brother, Mohd Bashir, just above the landslide. Inside, women gathered to mourn while men quietly received visitors offering condolences. Verses from the Qur’an echoed through the house.

“I built that house for my family,” Latief said, holding up pictures of his 16-year-old son Sajjad Ahmed, an aspiring cricketer, whose body was still missing. Days before the disaster, the family recorded videos together.

As mourners gathered, news spread that another body had been found several miles down the river; the room fell silent as another funeral procession passed through the village.

Among those searching was Mohammad Razak, 45, who had spent four days combing the river with a team of volunteers. “We’ve been searching every bend of the river,” he said. “We’re still hoping we’ll find them.”

Murrah was among the worst-hit places after a series of cloudbursts, flash floods and landslides swept Jammu and Kashmir this month, killing at least 28 people. Scientists say rising temperatures are increasing the likelihood of short, intense rainfall events across the western Himalayas. In steep mountainous terrain, these rains can trigger rapid flooding and landslides, putting remote communities at increased risk. For mountain communities, the climate crisis is also exacerbating longstanding geographical and social vulnerabilities.

The destruction stretched far beyond Murrah. About 30 miles away in Rajouri, the Manawar Tawi River burst its banks, washing away roads, dozens of vehicles and the town’s main Bela bus station.

Low-lying settlements along the riverbank were submerged in mud and debris. Several houses collapsed across the Pir Panjal mountains, livestock were swept away and hundreds of families were displaced.

About 180 miles north, in Gurez Valley near the line of control with Pakistan-administered Kashmir, residents say they are seeing the same pattern. A cloudburst in Achoora village on 20 July damaged the crops of 11 families and blocked the valley’s only road.

Residents say increasingly erratic rainfall is disrupting farming and making traditional livelihoods more precarious. It followed a series of cloudbursts that hit Gurez and neighbouring Tulail over the past month, damaging homes, farmland, bridges, and roads.

“People knew when the snow would come and when to plant crops,” said Aamir Asghar Khan, 26, a resident of Achoora. “Nothing seems predictable any more. The rain is getting more intense every year, and the frequent cloudbursts are threatening our livelihoods.”

Heavy rainfall also triggered devastating floods and landslides in Ladakh and across the border in Pakistan-administered Gilgit-Baltistan, reinforcing concerns that increasingly erratic weather is affecting communities across the western Himalayas.

The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (Icimod) said the western Himalayas were experiencing frequent bursts of intense rainfall capable of triggering floods, landslides and cloudbursts. Accelerating glacier melt is likely to increase flood risks in the short term before reducing water availability in coming decades.

“The challenge our mountain communities face is twofold – too much water at times and too little at others,” an expert from Icimod said. “Adaptation requires work on both fronts, managing flood risk and water scarcity together.”

ICIMOD said priorities included expanding community-based early warning systems, installing more weather stations in high-altitude areas, restoring damaged watersheds and designing roads and other infrastructure for future weather conditions rather than historical weather patterns.

Dr Suheel Rasool Mir, a Kashmir-based sociologist who studies Indigenous communities in Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, said pastoral communities were among the first to bear the consequences of erratic weather as their livelihoods relied directly on forests, rivers, grazing lands and seasonal migration.

“For Gujjar, Bakarwal and Dard-Shin communities, these disasters are not simply natural hazards,” he said. “As climate extremes become more frequent, they lose not only homes and livestock but also the ecological knowledge and ancestral livelihoods that have sustained them for generations.”

For Latief back in Murrah, only one hope remained. “I just want to find them,” he said. “Then we can bury our family together.”

title: Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones
excerpt:
People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100

Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the borde...
body_text:
People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100

Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged of about 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.

On Tuesday, as interior ministers from across the EU joined an emergency videoconference to grapple with the lingering tensions, the focus on the Moroccan side of the border with Ceuta was on the harrowing death toll.

At least 88 people have died in Ceuta, according to local officials, and another 11 in Morocco, while dozens of others remain missing.

“I have just one son,” said Hadijja, who had been waiting at the border since Saturday, scanning the steady stream of returnees for any sign of her 23-year-old son. “I haven’t had any news of him; he’s not answering his mobile phone.”

She had travelled to the border from her home in Tangier, surmising that her unemployed son was among those who had made the crossing. “He didn’t tell me he was going to cross,” she said. “This is a tragedy.”

An estimated 70,000 people who arrived late last week in Ceuta had been returned to Morocco in recent days, Spain’s interior minister said Tuesday.

Referencing posts on TikTok, Facebook and WhatsApp that had claimed Morocco was letting people cross the border, people arrived at Fnideq by foot or packed into buses and cars as they joined the surge of people crossing into Spain.

Madrid sprang into action, working with Rabat to return the vast majority of those who crossed within 48 hours, even as it fended off a political crisis sparked by calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

As they returned to Moroccan soil, some said they had come home voluntarily. “I was hungry for days and filled with fear,” said Abselam, 19, from Kenitra in north-western Morocco.

A Ceuta resident had eventually taken him in, giving him food and a place to sleep, before he decided to return home. “It’s not worth it, there aren’t jobs for everyone.”

Others said they had been forced out of the Spanish territory. “The police surrounded a group of us and escorted us all the way towards the border,” said Simo, 21, from Tetuan. “We didn’t really have a choice.”

In recent days, NGOs across Spain have voiced concerns that some of those who crossed into Ceuta and who were eligible for international protection were being returned before being allowed to exercise their right to request asylum.

On Tuesday the Spanish government estimated that 2,000 people who had made the crossing were still in Ceuta. The tally includes at least 862 children who have been registered as unaccompanied minors, as Unicef Spain warned that dozens more could still be wandering the city’s streets unprotected.

“Many small children crossed over; we don’t know how many have disappeared,” Susana Hidalgo, a migration expert for the organisation, told the broadcaster TVE. The result was a “tremendously difficult” situation in Ceuta.

“There are many families on the other side of the border looking for their sons and daughters,” she said, while in Ceuta “there are 10- and 12-year-old children asking for phones so they can call their mothers and tell them they’re OK.”

Spanish police said on Tuesday they had set up an office in Ceuta to gather reports of missing people.

The concerns over the fate of unaccompanied children in Ceuta were heightened on Tuesday after Spanish media published a video that appeared to show a boy age 12 crying as he begged a soldier not to send him back to Morocco. After several bystanders intervened, pointing out that Spanish law impeded children from being deported alone, the operation – which played out just metres from the border – was halted.

Days after the sudden influx, questions continue to linger as to what led to the mass crossing. Morocco has faced mounting accusations over the role it may have played. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of Ceuta, said earlier this week.

The insinuation was rejected by a senior Moroccan official. “It’s simplistic to say that Morocco should just have used force to stop them. That is to completely misunderstand this phenomenon,” the official told AFP.

“At a certain point, the Moroccan law enforcement forces could no longer confront the migrants because the numbers were very large” and because “the pull effect was very strong,” he added. “Could Spain, seeing them coming, have done something to stop them simply using weapons and security forces? That’s not possible.”

In a statement published on Sunday, Morocco’s interior ministry laid blame with the “exploitation of the digital sphere” and “the spread of misinformation” to explain the mass crossing.

Spanish intelligence sources have suggested the influx could be traced to a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported.

The Moroccan official said Rabat had sought to warn Madrid about the repercussions of the ruling. “We started engaging with the Spanish side around 22-23 July, when the networks began talking about this,” the official told AFP. “We explained that this ruling was going to create a problem. And it did create a problem.”

The claim was rejected by Spain’s migration minister, Elma Saiz. “At no point was there any evidence, any report that alerted us to the magnitude of this unprecedented event,” she told reporters in Madrid.

The uncertainty hovering over what exactly transpired extended to Fnideq, where the relatives gathered at the border spoke in hushed tones of what could have happened to their loved ones.

Many held on to hope, citing the trickle of good-news stories that had emerged in recent days, such as that of Fatima, who had spent the day waiting at the border with her family for a glimpse of her brother, who had crossed into Ceuta days earlier.

“My brother’s phone had run out of battery, but yesterday he borrowed the phone of a Spaniard to call me,” she said. “He told me he would come back this morning, so here we are waiting. I’m sure he’ll arrive soon.”

title: Lindsay Clancy strikes evidence deal as fingerprint gap opens trial debate, expert says
excerpt:
Lindsay Clancy told a Massachusetts judge she knowingly and voluntarily agreed to a set of stipulated facts, relieving prosecutors of the burden of proving those facts at her murder trial.

Lindsay Cl...
body_text:
Lindsay Clancy told a Massachusetts judge she knowingly and voluntarily agreed to a set of stipulated facts, relieving prosecutors of the burden of proving those facts at her murder trial.

Lindsay Clancy spoke directly in court Tuesday, repeatedly answering, "Yes, Your Honor," as she agreed to let prosecutors treat certain forensic facts as established hours before a state police trooper testified that investigators recovered no usable fingerprints from a knife or three exercise bands.

The developments narrowed the Massachusetts mother’s murder trial toward its central dispute: whether Clancy was criminally responsible when her three children were killed inside the family’s Duxbury home.

Before jurors entered the courtroom, Judge William Sullivan questioned Clancy about a stipulation covering certain evidence.

HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

"You understand that by signing the stipulation, you’re agreeing that the Commonwealth does not have to prove these certain facts that are contained in the stipulation," Sullivan said. "Do you understand that?"

Defendant Lindsay Clancy listens during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP, Pool)

Asked whether anyone had forced or threatened her to accept the agreement, Clancy said, "No, Your Honor."

Sullivan found that Clancy was competent and had entered the stipulation "knowingly, intelligently, voluntarily and willingly."

LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington said the agreement would prevent prosecutors from calling dozens of witnesses solely to establish the chain of custody for blood, bodily fluids, exercise bands and DNA evidence.

"We have not been contesting the government’s case in chief, if you will," Reddington said.

The stipulation is not a guilty plea or an admission that Clancy was criminally responsible for the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.

WATCH: Former prosecutor explains strategy behind Lindsay Clancy evidence agreement

Margaret McLean, a former criminal prosecutor and trial attorney who teaches law at Boston College’s Carroll School of Management, said the agreement allows the defense to steer jurors away from repetitive forensic testimony and toward Clancy’s mental state.

LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

"The legal strategy behind the move by the defense is to steer the jury’s focus away from the horrific nature of the acts and to that central issue of criminal intent, or what we would call mens rea," McLean told Fox News Digital.

McLean said Clancy’s measured responses Tuesday should not be taken as evidence of her mental condition on Jan. 24, 2023.

"She sounded rational. She understands what she’s doing," McLean said. "But remember, the Commonwealth’s burden of proof is to prove that she was sane beyond a reasonable doubt at the time the crimes were committed -- not today, not two weeks ago."

WATCH: Trooper details crime scene evidence collection at Lindsey Clancy's home

Later, Massachusetts State Police Trooper Jonathan O’Loughlin testified about examining a knife and three exercise bands collected from the home.

HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

O’Loughlin said the knife contained an area of friction-ridge impression, but investigators could not use it to identify anyone.

"There was not enough characteristics or minutia to do any comparison," O’Loughlin said, adding that the impression had "no value."

Defendant Lindsay Clancy on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, the fifth day of testimony at Plymouth Superior Court for her murder trial. Clancy is charged with three counts of murder in connection with the death of her three young children in 2023 at their Duxbury home. Clancy says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and is not criminally responsible. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

The yellow, black and blue exercise bands similarly produced no impressions suitable for comparison.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

"The bottom line is that you didn’t get any fingerprints," Reddington said.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

Lindsay Clancy's three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. (Lindsay Marie Clancy facebook)

O’Loughlin said fingerprints are "very, very, very fragile" and can be affected by an object’s texture, environmental conditions, movement, grip strength or whether a surface was wiped.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

McLean said the absence of identifiable prints could make jurors wonder whether gloves were used or the items were wiped, potentially viewing the missing prints as evidence of planning.

The defense, she said, can counter that jurors must not "speculate on something that’s not in evidence."

"They can use their common sense when they go to the table and they deliberate," McLean said, "but they can’t speculate [about] things that are not in the evidence."

Sarah Rumpf-Whitten is a U.S. Writer at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to sarah.rumpf@fox.com and on X @s_rumpfwhitten

title: Big money propels Dem megachurch pastor to victory in longshot Kansas Senate bid
excerpt:
Democratic primaries test progressive candidates as James Carville warns against far-left extremism ahead of the August elections.

Kansas Democrats have made their choice in one of the most crowded p...
body_text:
Democratic primaries test progressive candidates as James Carville warns against far-left extremism ahead of the August elections.

Kansas Democrats have made their choice in one of the most crowded primary battles in the nation and are backing a political newcomer with an eye-popping campaign war chest.

Adam Hamilton emerged victorious in an 11-way primary Tuesday night in the race to take on incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., who is running for a second term in the upper chamber.

And he has a line of attack against Hamilton already teed up.

DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE

Adam Hamilton cleared a field of 11 hopefuls to secure the Democratic nomination in the race to beat Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan. (Gerri Hernandez/Hamilton for Senate)

"Look, this guy is a woke, big megachurch pastor," Marshall told Fox News Digital. "He's too woke for Kansas. I think all we have to do is share his own sermons … with the Kansas people, and they're gonna realize that he's too woke for Kansas."

History is on the side of Marshall, who previously served four years in the House before making the leap to the Senate in 2020. That’s because Kansas has not sent a Democrat to the Senate in nearly a century. The last time was in the 1930s, when Kansans elected former Sen. George McGill. He only served one term before being ousted by a Republican.

TRUMP DEMAND PUTS VULNERABLE REPUBLICANS IN IMPOSSIBLE SPOT AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

Still, he’s not resting on his laurels as he stares down another likely funding disadvantage.

National Republicans aren’t dumping resources into Kansas like they are in other states, given that Marshall is a strong incumbent and valuable campaign cash is needed in tougher contests in Texas, Maine and Ohio.

While Kansas is not on Senate Republicans’ radar as a battleground state, there is big money flowing in that could make Marshall’s bid for another term complicated.

SUPREME COURT STRIKES DOWN LIMIT ON PARTY CAMPAIGN SPENDING IN COORDINATION WITH CANDIDATES

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., is running for a second term in the upper chamber. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Hamilton, who leads the nation’s largest United Methodist church and congregation, has raised just north of $4.1 million since launching his campaign in February, according to financial filings with the Federal Election Commission.

Marshall, on the other hand, has raised just over $6.2 million during this cycle.

"Well, this is probably why my staff tells me, no matter what the polls show, they tell me that we're down by three points, and we did get outspent about four to one last time around. Regardless, we're gonna keep working hard," Marshall said.

And as precious campaign resources flow to other marquee races during this cycle, where the GOP has more vulnerable incumbents up for reelection than Democrats, Marshall isn’t asking for a handout.

He wants the resources from major GOP campaign arms, like the National Republican Senatorial Committee or the GOP leadership-aligned Senate Leadership Fund, to stay put.

"I guess we're trying to not need to do that," Marshall said. "That's what our hope is, is that they won't need to do that. Leader McConnell was super helpful last time. So, you know, they're keeping tabs on this. We got to, you know, we're all one, big happy family here, so we're hoping we don't need them."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Australia news live: ASX hits record high, with investors bullish on peace; brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet appears before Icac inquiry
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian shares have rallied to a record high in early trading after optimism about peace negotiations in the Middle East buoyed global m...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian shares have rallied to a record high in early trading after optimism about peace negotiations in the Middle East buoyed global markets.

The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 spiked above the 9,200 point mark shortly after the market opened this morning, surpassing an intraday record set in late February.

Prices then eased to trade at 9,150 points by late morning.

The ASX has been pulled around by global events in recent months, with the Iran conflict and fears of an AI bubble leading to wild swings.

The recent bullish sentiment has outweighed concerns over inflation, which typically drag stock prices down. There have also been multiple past instances of failed negotiations between the US and Iran.

Market strategist Michael McCarthy, from trading platform Moomoo, says “while stock investors may be ignoring bad news while buying good news” there has been a flow of strong US company earnings reports to support stock prices.

The latest bout of market optimism was sparked by comments by US and Qatari officials saying progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz.

The main US index, the S&P 500, rallied to a record high overnight, led by a surging technology sector.

NSW police required to switch on body cameras under new policy

New South Wales police officers carrying out operational duties will be required to wear and activate body cameras under a new policy.

The change follows a key recommendation from the Law Enforcement Conduct Commission’s review of the force’s body-worn video policy and practice, prompted by a series of serious incidents in which officers failed to activate available cameras.

Under the new policy, officers must activate their body-worn cameras in most operational situations, unless doing so “is reasonable impracticable or an exemption applies”.

If an officer is not wearing a camera, fails to switch it on, or turns it off during a job, they will have to provide an explanation.

Chief Commissioner Peter Johnson welcomed the change, calling it “a very important development” that should “increase public confidence” in the force. He said:

double quotation markThe knowledge that interactions between police and community members are being recorded helps to keep both the officer and the community safe. The use of body worn cameras also promotes officer accountability by enabling the NSW Police Force and the Commission to effectively scrutinise officers’ actions where there are allegations of police misconduct.

The NSW Police Force says it has now implemented most of the Commission’s 15 recommendations.

NSW Liberal leader backs in shadow attorney general who admitted to leaking confidential report to Reformers

The NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, says she will not make a decision about the future of shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, after he admitted to Icac to leaking a confidential draft copy of a parliamentary inquiry report to a member of conservative right faction group the Reformers.

Yesterday, Tudehope, who is also leader of the Liberals in the upper house but has stepped aside from his roles during the inquiry after being called as a witness, admitted to leaking the confidential parliamentary document from an inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe. Members of the Reformers avoided being served summons to appear before the inquiry.

At a press conference this morning, Sloane, who has said she will not provide running commentary on Icac’s investigation, said yesterday’s evidence had not changed her position and she would make a decision about Tudehope’s future as shadow attorney general “once Icac proceedings have finalised”. She said:

double quotation markDamien cooperated with the inquiry. He was thanked by the inquiry, and he was released from his summons. The leaking of a report is never good. It’s a standard that I don’t accept. I spoke to Damien about that this morning, but the status remains that Damien is not in my shadow cabinet for the remainder of these hearings, and that’s appropriate. It’s not because he’s accused of anything wrong. It’s not because he’s a person of interest by the inquiry.

It’s because, quite simply, as my shadow attorney general, there’s a perceived conflict of interest. He is close to many of the parties involved, and he is in effect our spokesperson for Icac. So on that basis, he will remain, and I won’t pre-empt the outcomes of the inquiry.

Australian shares have rallied to a record high in early trading after optimism about peace negotiations in the Middle East buoyed global markets.

The benchmark S&P/ASX 200 spiked above the 9,200 point mark shortly after the market opened this morning, surpassing an intraday record set in late February.

Prices then eased to trade at 9,150 points by late morning.

The ASX has been pulled around by global events in recent months, with the Iran conflict and fears of an AI bubble leading to wild swings.

The recent bullish sentiment has outweighed concerns over inflation, which typically drag stock prices down. There have also been multiple past instances of failed negotiations between the US and Iran.

Market strategist Michael McCarthy, from trading platform Moomoo, says “while stock investors may be ignoring bad news while buying good news” there has been a flow of strong US company earnings reports to support stock prices.

The latest bout of market optimism was sparked by comments by US and Qatari officials saying progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz.

The main US index, the S&P 500, rallied to a record high overnight, led by a surging technology sector.

SpaceX rocket hours away from crashing into the moon

A four-tonne piece of a SpaceX rocket that has been floating in space since last year is set to unintentionally crash into the moon at high speed on Wednesday, a collision that poses no danger to Earth but will leave behind a new lunar crater and afford an opportunity for further scientific research.

The ​school-bus-size object is the second stage of a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket that had launched a lunar lander from Firefly Aerospace toward the moon in January 2025.

The rocket body ⁠is due to hit the moon about 4.35pm Sydney time.

The NSW government has formally accepted all recommendations from a coronial inquest into the stabbing deaths of six people at Bondi Junction shopping centre in 2024.

The final report into the attack made 13 recommendations directed to the government, 11 of which it will accept in full and two in principle. They include a new health-led response model for mental heath emergencies funded with $270m over the next 10 years and stronger community mental health services, among others.

“The Government’s response outlines the significant work already underway across agencies to strengthen mental health care, enhance emergency preparedness and response, improve community safety, and deliver on the Coroner’s recommendations,” a press release reads.

NSW health minister Ryan Park said in a statement:

double quotation markThe Government’s response continues our work to strengthen mental health services, improve access to care and ensure people with severe and complex mental illness receive the support they need earlier and closer to home.

We are investing in reforms that improve coordination across the health system and help people access the right care at the right time.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny hearings resumed this morning.

Today’s witness is Reformers member Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet.

Icac is investigating whether Liberal figures including Jean-Claude solicited or accepted illegal donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the Liberal party, a practice known as branch stacking, which is not itself illegal.

Icac is investigating another allegation that Liberal figures including his brother, Charles Perrottet, solicited or accepted donations from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif.

The inquiry has heard that Jean-Claude and Charles avoided being served summons to appear at a parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe. Yesterday’s witness, NSW shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, who admitted to leaking a confidential draft report from the parliamentary inquiry to another Reformer, claimed to have discussed with Dominic Perrottet that Jean-Claude was in Fiji during the 2023 inquiry.

Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing, while Jean-Claude and Charles have previously denied any wrongdoing.

Victorian premier will read report from corruption watchdog ‘carefully’

Ben Carroll held a press conference after the release of the report by Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog into the former Andrews government’s dealings with United Firefighters Union and its secretary Peter Marshall.

The Victorian premier said he would “read the report carefully” and give “Victorians the action and the answers they deserve”. Carroll went on:

double quotation markThis is poor behaviour. It is intolerable.

I will take action. I will accept the recommendations and get on with implementing [them].

Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog has tabled a long-awaited report into the former Daniel Andrews government’s dealings with the United Firefighters Union and its secretary Peter Marshall.

The Operation Richmond report did not find that any individuals engaged in corrupt conduct, but it found that senior members of the Andrews government engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct in their dealings with Marshall when negotiating pay deals for the Country Fire Authority and Metropolitan Fire Brigade, and their later amalgamation into Fire Services Victoria.

This included “actions contrary to policy, procedure and codes of conduct, deliberate attempts to conceal and mislead, and the misuse of information.”

The Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (Ibac) found the government made an “undisclosed deal” with Marshall, “to the exclusion of other key stakeholders,” which allowed him to “exert extraordinary influence over the negotiations” for both the CFA and MFB enterprise bargaining agreements.

Ibac also found that Marshall was granted “privileged access” to responsible ministers.

The final release of the findings comes after years of legal attempts by the UFU to keep the report secret, including a high court challenge. The investigation first began in 2018 following a tip-off that Marshall “blackmailed or otherwise compromised” Andrews “to change his position on the CFA EBA”. Ibac found no evidence of blackmail and did not substantiate the allegation, which both Andrews and Marshall denied.

Victorian premier says he wants Suburban Rail Loop to be ‘most cost effective it can be’

On the Suburban Rail Loop, Carroll says he’s not going to be “ripping up contracts” but wants to ensure the project is “the most cost effective it can be”. So far the state has signed about $14.5bn worth of contracts for SRL East – a 26km stretch of tunnels between Cheltenham and Box Hill – with tunnelling to begin soon.

double quotation markThis project is proceeding, but I want it done in a cost-effective, transparent way, making sure Victorians know that every dollar we spend on their behalf is treated with respect.

Host Raf Epstein asked: “Does cost-effective mean you’ll spend less each year? Are you going to slow down spending on the SRL?”

double quotation markCarroll: “Raf, I’ve got no announcements to make on that today except to say this is a project for the state, just like Airport Rail, just like Melton electrification. I want a more integrated approach to Victoria’s transport system.”

Epstein: “That sounds like you are going to slow down that project so you can spend some of those dollars elsewhere.”

Carroll: “Raf, I am focused on a statewide integrated public transport system. Orbital rail is an important part of Victoria’s future. Airport Rail, as someone who used to watch the planes as a young boy and still in my house now, Airport Rail under my premiership will be my focus and the number one project for our state.”

Victoria’s new premier, Ben Carroll, gave his first broadcast interview with ABC Radio Melbourne’s Raf Epstein this morning, where he was grilled about his involvement in last week’s leadership spill.

He said it was “not an easy decision” to put his hand up for the leadership and he only did so after a group of colleagues had already told Jacinta Allan they had lost confidence in her.

double quotation markEpstein: “So you had nothing to do with it?”

Carroll also stressed that the newly created minister for AI would not mean a free-for-all regarding datacentres. He said:

double quotation markWhat is clear with artificial intelligence and datacentres is that it’s off the leash, so to speak, Raf, and I think we need to put working people and the people we represent into that equation. And I don’t think they are at the moment. Whether it’s AI or datacentres, I want to make sure it’s not just free rein.

When asked who let AI off the leash, Carroll replied:

double quotation markThis is what happens with the big disruptors. We know [this is] the biggest disruptor happening to society right now. We’ve seen it with other things, Uber, transport. But what I want to do is make sure we have a strong, vibrant datacentre industry [and] a strong, vibrant artificial intelligence industry, but with the guardrails and the regulatory reform. I have tasked the incoming minister for artificial intelligence and digital economy – that is his first priority: putting workers front and centre of this massive economic transformation for society.

While she recently returned to the Southern California franchise and stars in "The Real Housewives Ultimate Girls Trip: Roaring 20th" to commemorate two decades of the Bravo cult-classic, Gunvalson admitted that her own family didn't receive the same kind of network treatment that she has over the years.

Gunvalson, 64, confessed to The Hollywood Reporter that daughter Briana Culberson wants "nothing to do" with the series, years after her military husband's portrayal on the reality show.

REALITY TV STARS CLASH OVER WHAT REALLY DESTROYED THEIR MARRIAGE AFTER SHOCKING BEDROOM CONFESSION

Vicki Gunvalson starred on the first episode of "Real Housewives of Orange County" in 2006, and recently returned to the franchise after a short hiatus. (Jason Howard)

Briana, 39, appeared in a handful of episodes with her mother through the years, and was allegedly asked to return for season 20, but she had no interest in returning to the cameras.

She allegedly told Bravo patriarch Andy Cohen to "please lose my number," when asked about a special appearance.

REALITY STAR'S DAUGHTER ARRESTED ON ASSAULT CHARGE IN NEW JERSEY STEMMING FROM ALLEGED DISPUTE

"My children are now 39 and 40," Gunvalson said. "My son did a film this year. My daughter wants nothing to do with it."

Briana last appeared on the network during Season 18 of "Watch What Happens Live." (Bravo)

"Her husband just got back from the Marine Corps — six tours overseas — and he’s got some PTSD, and they really showed a bad light of him. She just was like, 'Mom, I want nothing to do with it.' I’m like, 'Can you do a cameo? Can you come on for a little bit?'

She added, "Andy even called her for this season and she was like, 'Please lose my number.' What the show did to their family was not good."

Briana and husband Ryan Culberson have four children together and have been married for 15 years.

Briana and Ryan Culberson have four children together and have been married for 15 years. (Paul Archuleta)

Gunvalson's son, Michael, 40, recently appeared on a "RHOC" episode, where he confessed that he hadn't seen his sister in eight years.

"I mean, I haven’t even met two of her kids," he said. "Not good."

She added in a confessional, "It absolutely sucks that my kids live far away. Mike’s in Spain, Briana lives in Oklahoma. They talk all the time, they FaceTime. But it’s definitely better to be in person."

"I see other families have their kids over on Sunday dinner, and I don’t have that. It’s not what I’d ever planned, but it’s their life."

The original cast of "The Real Housewives of Orange County" included Jeana Keough, Lauri Waring, Jo De La Rosa, Kimberly Bryant and Vicki Gunvalson  (Chris McPherson)

"Housewives" woes hit Gunvalson hard as she admitted her ex-husband once gave her an ultimatum between their marriage and the show – and made a decision she now regrets.

"It killed mine," she said of the "RHOC" impact on her marriage. "When Scott [Dunlop] approached me and Donn [Gunvalson, Vicki’s then-husband] at the time about doing this pilot, Donn’s like, 'There’s no way we’re doing this in our family.'"

"He was like, 'Anybody that goes on TV is going to get divorced.' I’m like, 'We’re not going to get divorced. We’re fine.' And obviously, fast-forward, we got divorced."

Vicki and Donn Gunvalson's relationship and subsequent divorce was documented on "The Real Housewives of Orange County." (Brett Ascarelli)

She added, "My family was more important than the show, and it broke apart."

Fellow housewife Porsha Williams gave a few words of wisdom and said, "Two things can be true. The show can strain a marriage, but it can also reveal things about that marriage — or about yourself — that you needed to know."

Gunvalson noted, "If the marriage is weak, it’s going to fall apart."

title: Armed man arrested at Trump’s California golf course
excerpt:
Jeanine John Taele allegedly took photos and videos of property days before president’s visit

Los Angeles county sheriff’s deputies arrested an armed California man over the weekend who was seen surv...
body_text:
Jeanine John Taele allegedly took photos and videos of property days before president’s visit

Los Angeles county sheriff’s deputies arrested an armed California man over the weekend who was seen surveilling Donald Trump’s golf course in Rancho Palos Verdes, days before the president was set to arrive there for an event with the Republican National Committee (RNC).

Plainclothes federal agents reported Jeanine John Taele, 38, as a “suspicious individual”, after they observed him on Sunday taking photographs and videos of the golf grounds, located in a coastal town south of Los Angeles, according to county officials.

After the sheriff’s deputies detained Taele, they found a loaded magazine in his pocket and a loaded pistol in his car. Investigators obtained a search warrant for Taele’s home in Downey, citing “the potential security implications”, and recovered a trove of weapons from the residence including a .45-caliber pistol, body armor, an illegally modified AR-type pistol, among others, officials said.

In Taele’s house, law enforcement officers also found “multiple notebooks containing concerning statements”. The nature of the remarks remains unclear.

Taele has been arrested for carrying a concealed firearm and possession of prohibited ammunition. Investigators have put the case before the Los Angeles county district attorney’s office to determine if and what charges will be filed.

Trump is expected to land in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. A White House spokesperson reportedly described the trip as an opportunity for the president to draw contrast between his administration’s “commonsense agenda” and the “radical policies” of Democratic leaders such as the California governor, Gavin Newsom, with whom he has verbally sparred online.

Regarding Taele’s arrest, the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department said on Tuesday they had identified no credible threat to its communities.

Trump has been the target of violence in the past.

In April, Cole Tomas Allen, a California man with alleged grievances against the Trump administration, sprinted through a security checkpoint at the White House correspondents’s association dinner, where the president was in attendance, before being apprehended by Secret Service agents. He has been charged with an attempt to assassinate a US president, to which he has pleaded not guilty.

In July 2024, a gunman opened fire at a campaign rally where Trump was speaking then as a presidential nominee. A crowd member was killed and a bullet grazed Trump’s ear. Federal agents fatally shot the suspected shooter, 20-year-old Thomas Matthew Crooks. The FBI found no clear motive behind the deadly shooting.

Ryan Routh was recently sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of attempting to assassinate Trump on a Florida golf course in September 2024. Prosecutors said Routh spent weeks plotting to kill Trump before aiming a rifle through shrubbery as the then Republican presidential candidate played golf at his West Palm Beach country club.

title: Missouri rejects citizens’ bid for vote on Trump-backed redistricting plan
excerpt:
Missouri’s top election official has rejected a petition for a referendum on new congressional districts

Missouri’s top election official has rejected a citizens’ petition seeking a statewide referen...
body_text:
Missouri’s top election official has rejected a petition for a referendum on new congressional districts

Missouri’s top election official has rejected a citizens’ petition seeking a statewide referendum on the state’s redistricting plan backed by Donald Trump.

Supporters of the referendum had submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures in an effort to force a November election on whether to use a new US House map approved by the Republican-led state legislature. But the Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, asserted on Tuesday that the petition was void because congressional redistricting plans cannot be subject to voter referendums.

The number of petition signatures submitted did not matter, Hoskins said, because “challenging a congressional map is unconstitutional under Missouri law”.

A group backing the referendum effort said it would contest Hoskins’ decision in court.

“Secretary of State Hoskins is making a last desperate attempt to silence the people’s voice in Missouri,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement, while asserting there were more than enough signatures to qualify the referendum for the ballot.

Missouri was the second Republican-led state, after Texas, to respond to Trump’s call last year to redraw congressional districts to the GOP’s advantage in hopes of holding on to the party’s slim House majority in the midterm elections.

The new map, which is being used in Tuesday’s primaries, dramatically reshapes the Kansas City-based fifth congressional district, held by longtime Democratic representative Emanuel Cleaver, by stretching it into rural central Missouri to give it a Republican tilt. Republicans already hold six of Missouri’s eight congressional seats and hope to gain another under the new map.

Hoskins shoots down amendment on citizen initiatives

Hoskins also rejected a potential November ballot measure seeking to fortify the initiative process.

The proposed amendment would bar the legislature from making it harder to qualify citizen initiatives for the ballot or approve them at an election. It also would make it harder for the legislature to reverse or amend voter-approved initiatives by requiring an 80% vote in both the house and senate, instead of the current simple majority.

Although supporters had submitted thousands of signatures, Hoskins asserted that the petition violated a constitutional prohibition against rolling multiple subjects and sections of the constitution into a single amendment.

The Respect Missouri Voters coalition said it would take legal action to try to get its amendment on the ballot.

“This brazen disregard for the will of the people is exactly why the people of Missouri came together to gather signatures ... because we are sick of these games in Jefferson City,” said Bob Johnson, a coalition member and former Republican state senator.

For both the redistricting referendum and the citizen initiative measure, Hoskins released opinions from the Republican attorney general, Catherine Hanaway, laying out the rationale for his decisions.

People Not Politicians, the group sponsoring the referendum drive, submitted more than 300,000 signatures to the secretary of state’s office in December. Local election officials reviewed the signatures’ validity over the ensuing months and approved significantly more than the roughly 111,000 needed to qualify for the ballot.

But Hoskins waited until the last day allowed under state law to announce his decision about the referendum – a move that let the new districts be used in the meantime.

Hoskins had long signaled that he was likely to reject the referendum. He asked a federal court last fall to block the referendum petition from being submitted, arguing that congressional redistricting is not subject to a referendum under the US and Missouri constitutions. A judge dismissed the lawsuit as premature, noting in a December ruling that Hoskins had the authority to reject the petition himself if he thought it was unconstitutional.

When Missouri candidates began filing for office in February, Hoskins said they were doing so under the new districts and told the Associated Press that “the referendum process was never meant to be used for redistricting”.

If Hoskins is wrong, and a court orders him to place the redistricting referendum on the ballot, it’s unclear what that means for the 2026 elections. Would candidates who win Tuesday’s primaries be allowed to continue running under the new districts in November while voters simultaneously decide whether those districts can be used in future elections? Would candidates run in different districts for the general election than were used in the primaries? Or would courts order a do-over for the congressional primaries using the state’s prior congressional districts?

Missouri’s mid-decade redistricting effort already has been among the most litigated nationally, triggering about a dozen lawsuits over the past year.

Legislative voting districts typically are redrawn at the start of each decade, immediately after a census. But Trump’s call for Republicans to redraw districts to their advantage led to an unusual outbreak of mid-decade mapmaking. The redistricting effort gained additional steam when the US supreme court struck down a majority Black congressional district in Louisiana in late April, prompting Republicans in several southern states to also redraw districts that had large minority populations.

All told, Republicans think they could win as many as 16 additional seats from new House maps enacted in eight states – Texas, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Florida, Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama. Democrats, whose counterattack faced several setbacks, think they could win up to six additional seats from new districts in California and Utah.

Voters ultimately will determine whether the new districts perform as intended. Even with redistricting, Republicans are facing headwinds. The president’s party historically has lost congressional seats in the midterms, and Trump’s poor approval ratings could provide an extra hurdle for Republican candidates.

Nearly 145 million people – about two of every five US residents – live in states with new congressional districts for this election. Additional states are considering redistricting before the 2028 elections. Maryland lawmakers voted on Tuesday to place an amendment on November’s ballot that could pave the way for mid-decade redistricting.

title: NFL executives, coaches put Shedeur Sanders last in QB rankings in survey: 'Shouldn't lose to him'
excerpt: Caleb Williams is coming off an impressive season, leading the Chicago Bears to the playoffs. Danny Parkins asks if Caleb and Chicago Bears HC Ben Johnson can build on this success, and if Shedeur San...
body_text:
Caleb Williams is coming off an impressive season, leading the Chicago Bears to the playoffs. Danny Parkins asks if Caleb and Chicago Bears HC Ben Johnson can build on this success, and if Shedeur Sanders will be the starting QB for the Cleveland ...

Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders had flashes of great play when he finally got a chance to start during his rookie season in 2025.

But it doesn’t seem to be enough in the eyes of executives and coaches around the league after The Athletic released its 2026 NFL quarterback tiers list, where Sanders was dead last among the 35 ranked signal callers.

"I’d sleep like a baby if I got to play him every week," an unnamed defensive coordinator in the report said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders (12) throws the ball against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on Nov. 23, 2025. (Kirby Lee/Imagn Images)

An executive added: "He’s inaccurate at all three levels. I can’t tell if he is going to get better, but there’s a huge gap between him and competent QB play."

The tiers list went from the best quarterbacks (Tier 1) to the worst (Tier 5) followed by a regular ranking vote. After gathering the surveys from the 50 executives and coaches, Sanders saw just one Tier 3 vote, while receiving 37 Tier 4 tallies and 12 Tier 5 votes.

"He’s not an on-time player, can’t really read through the coverages, is a little bit heavy-footed. He is thicker and harder to tackle than expected, but you shouldn’t lose to him," another coordinator added.

Sanders now finds himself in another quarterback battle at Browns training camp, this time with Deshaun Watson healthy and vying for the starting role in new head coach Todd Monken’s offense.

BROWNS COACH TODD MONKEN KEEPING QB COMPETITION OPEN AMID UNEVEN PRACTICE REPS, SHEDEUR SANDERS BUZZ

Sanders, who was named the starter for the remaining six games of the Browns’ 2025 season after winning his starting debut against the Las Vegas Raiders, threw for an even 1,400 yards with seven touchdowns, while giving up 10 interceptions.

But the Browns surely wanted to see a better completion rate, as he connected on just 56.6% of his throws.

Cleveland Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders (12) at the line of scrimmage in the third quarter at Bank of America Stadium. (Bob Donnan/Imagn Images)

Could Monken’s influence as an offensive-minded head coach help Sanders’ development with the Browns? One voter believes so.

"Todd Monken is a great reset in the same way Ben Johnson was a great reset in Chicago. Shedeur gets a fresh start with a no-nonsense, offensive-oriented coach who did a really good job with Lamar Jackson," the voter told the outlet.

"If Shedeur has really invested in himself to be a professional quarterback, studying the playbook and knowing his assignments and being able to get the offense in and out of the huddle at an efficient clip, which he could not do last year, then there might be some upside."

Monken still must make his QB1 clear, and he has been steadfast all offseason in saying there will be a true competition taking place in his first Browns camp. Sanders, Watson and Dillon Gabriel are battling each other as we speak.

Shedeur Sanders, No. 2 of the Cleveland Browns, throws a pass during mandatory minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus in Berea, Ohio, on June 9, 2026. (Nick Cammett/Getty Images)

Watson made it on the list, too, ranking 31st among the 35 quarterbacks. He did not play last season as he continued his recovery from an Achilles injury suffered in the 2024 campaign.

The Browns will get their first taste of competition on Aug. 15 when they face the Bears in their first preseason game.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Mom of 4 recovering after suspected spider bite leads to severe complications: reports

A Kansas mother of four is reportedly recovering after a suspected spider bite led to surgery, serious infections and ...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A Kansas mother of four is reportedly recovering after a suspected spider bite led to surgery, serious infections and a weeks-long hospital stay.

Britagne Miller, of Goddard — about 14 miles west of Wichita — said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children at Cheney Lake on May 28, when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her, according to local outlets KAKE and FOX Kansas.

Four days later, the area around one bite on her calf became swollen and painful, prompting her to seek medical care, FOX Kansas reported.

"This one kept swelling and swelling, and it was like, you know, a fire stir that's metal," Miller told KAKE. "It was like shooting down my leg into my foot, and it felt like it was being stabbed."

GIANT GOLDEN SPIDERS COULD SPREAD THIS SUMMER; EXPERTS DOWNPLAY HEALTH RISK

Britagne Miller said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children on May 28 when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

Miller was admitted to Wesley Hospital in Wichita on June 4 and underwent surgery, according to KAKE and a GoFundMe created by her husband, Jake Miller.

Her treatment was complicated by existing blood-clotting disorders, liver problems and allergies to certain medications, KAKE reported.

Miller later developed infections. Doctors also determined that she was suffering from end-stage liver failure and warned her family that her condition could be fatal, according to KAKE.

Miller, who chose to continue treatment rather than enter hospice care, said she remembers little from her time in intensive care, according to the outlet.

BULL BISON SENDS YELLOWSTONE VISITOR FLIPPING THROUGH THE AIR IN CAMPGROUND ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Britagne Miller said she remembers little from her time in intensive care. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

She was released from the hospital on July 11, and is continuing her recovery at home.

Miller now requires home health care, physical therapy and regular visits with specialists. She also hopes to receive a liver transplant but is not yet eligible to be placed on the transplant list, according to KAKE and the GoFundMe.

Doctors have not confirmed what kind of spider bit her, KAKE reported.

Dr. Raymond Cloyd, a horticultural entomologist at Kansas State University, told KAKE that the brown recluse and black widow are two venomous spiders commonly found in Kansas.

TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

Britagne Miller was released from the hospital on July 11, and is continuing her recovery at home. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)

Cloyd advised sealing cracks and using caution with boxes, shoes and other undisturbed items, KAKE reported.

"We know there is still a long road ahead, but we are holding on to hope that one day this season will be behind us, and she will be able to continue doing what she loves most — being a mom, and someday a grandmother," the GoFundMe states.

The Miller family could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for additional comment.

Sophia Compton is a Writer at Fox News Digital. Sophia was previously a business reporter covering finance, energy and tourism and has experience as a TV news producer. She graduated with a journalism degree in 2021 from the University of Hawaii at Manoa. Story tips can be sent to sophia.compton@fox.com.

title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud
excerpt:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília

Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp ...
body_text:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília

Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.

The Trump administration stopped short of expelling Viotti, a former senior United Nations official. But Washington warned that further diplomatic action remains possible if Brasília continues to withhold its approval for would-be ambassador Daniel Perez, a Florida Republican and close ally of the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” a state department spokesperson said.

The ambassador’s visa could be restored if Brazil accepts Perez’s appointment. “This is a reciprocal action,” the spokesperson said. “Should the ambassador leave the country, she would need to reapply for a visa.”

The dispute has become entangled with Brazil’s increasingly bitter election campaign, in which Lula, 80, is seeking a fourth, non-consecutive term against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, and a close political ally of Trump.

Brasília swiftly condemned the US action as part of a deliberate campaign to influence the election. Lula’s office said: “Today’s decision is not an isolated incident. It is part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, motivated by ideological reasons.”

Brazil also accused the US of breaching diplomatic norms by announcing Perez’s nomination before seeking Brasília’s consent. The Brazilian government said its consideration of the appointment was still under way, and that it had been made clear no decision would be taken before the first round of the election, on 4 October.

The Trump administration argues that Brazil has no right to interfere with the president’s choice of US ambassador to the country.

“President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world,” the state department said. “We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes.”

The latest confrontation follows Brazil’s refusal last month to issue visas to Riley Barnes, assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, and one of his senior aides.

The US officials had planned to visit Brasília from 27 to 30 July for meetings with government officials, religious leaders and others about election integrity, religious freedom and freedom of expression.

Washington described the trip as routine, and rejected Brazilian claims that it was intended to interfere in the election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” the state department said at the time.

Brasília has stood by its decision, saying the officials intended to cast doubt on the integrity of Brazil’s electronic voting system in what it called an “unacceptable attempt to interfere in the national political process”.

The row is particularly sensitive because Jair Bolsonaro and his supporters have spent years alleging, without evidence, that Brazil’s electronic voting system is vulnerable to fraud. He has been barred from standing for office and was convicted over a plot to overturn his defeat in the 2022 election.

The diplomatic confrontation is the latest in a series of clashes between Trump and Lula, whose governments have sharply diverged over Latin American politics, Venezuela, Cuba and the role of the US in the region.

Trump has repeatedly intervened in political contests across Latin America, while Lula has made national sovereignty a central theme of his campaign. The Brazilian president has blamed Rubio for some of the administration’s actions against his government, although he has sought to avoid a direct personal confrontation with Trump, and has said the two men got on well when they first met.

Economic pressure has added to the tensions. The Trump administration has imposed tariffs of up to 37.5% on thousands of Brazilian exports, citing what it says are unfair trade practices and failures to prevent forced labour. Lula’s government has rejected the allegations, and accused Trump’s administration of trying to help Bolsonaro’s political family.

The US has also classified Brazil’s two biggest drug-trafficking organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, a move opposed by Lula’s government.

Yet the state department insists that it still wants to restore a normal relationship with Brasília. “We want to be back in a situation where we have a normal, productive, transparent relationship with our colleagues,” a senior US official said.

title: Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed
excerpt:
Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign...
body_text:
Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

Almost 400 native Australian bird and mammal species have been assessed as being at a high risk – or worse – from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, a federal government assessment has revealed.

Some of Australia’s most beloved animals – including species of penguins, fur seals, quolls, dolphins, more than 300 birds and the Tasmanian devil – are considered at least high risk from the virus, meaning they could suffer “severe reduction in population size or viability” or worse if it reached them.

Five species are considered at extreme risk, meaning “unlikely to survive where the virus occurs”.

These are all birds that breed in single islands or groups of islands, such as the endangered Christmas Island frigatebird and the critically endangered herald petrel, which only breeds on Raine Island in the far north of the Great Barrier Reef.

More than 80 endangered and critically endangered species are also considered to be facing at least a high risk from an infection, suggesting that the H5N1 strain of bird flu will push them further towards extinction.

The federal government released the results of the assessment of more than 2,000 native species, carried out with Charles Darwin University and BirdLife Australia, on Tuesday evening. Nearly one in five have been rated as facing extreme, very high or high risk.

Australia’s three resident seals – the Australian fur seal, the New Zealand fur seal and the Australian sea lion – are all considered at very high risk. The Tasmanian devil and the eastern quoll, both assessed as high risk, are the land mammals at greatest threat.

The extent of the analysis and the number of species considered at high risk underlines expert fears for the threat to local wildlife.

Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter
