Anthropic says anyone who has been charged for a fraudulent purchase should contact its support site and the charges will be refunded.

Rutter has since been refunded by Anthropic, and the temporary refund from Metro Bank is due to be taken back by the bank.

Metro Bank told him in a letter that he had not received the service it expected its customers to get, and it offered him £300 by way of compensation.

Rutter says he intends to make a complaint about what happened to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

The bank says it has taken steps to prevent delays in cards being blocked.

Anyone who has been affected by an unauthorised card fraud is advised to contact their bank immediately and ask for a refund. They may then be asked to fill out forms detailing what happened.The FCA says the refund should be in a customer’s account by the end of the next business day.

title: Palestine weekly: Israel kills dozens in Gaza after Hamas disarmament deal
excerpt: United States President Donald Trump announced “a historic agreement” on July 30 for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, framed as the long-awaited move into the second phase of t...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump announced “a historic agreement” on July 30 for the disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza, framed as the long-awaited move into the second phase of the October 2025 “ceasefire” deal.

The agreement was negotiated through the Board of Peace, established by Trump to oversee post-war reconstruction and governance of Gaza.

However, Hamas negotiator Ghazi Hamad told Al Jazeera the Palestinian group would not implement the deal unless Israel fulfilled its obligations, which include halting attacks and withdrawing troops.

A spokesperson for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office, meanwhile, said Israeli forces would not withdraw until Hamas was fully disarmed.

With that fundamental deadlock unresolved, Israeli attacks on Gaza, which have characterised the 10-month “ceasefire”, continued, arguably with even greater intensity. Within days of the announcement of the “historic agreement”, Israeli strikes killed at least 19 Palestinians in a single day, bringing the weekend death toll in Gaza to 26.

Board of Peace envoy Nickolay Mladenov condemned the escalation without naming Israel directly: “Two days of strikes across Gaza have killed civilians and destroyed medical supplies that people depend on,” he said.

The attacks capped a month that was the deadliest in Gaza this year, and the deadliest for Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, in terms of Israeli settler attacks, since 2023.

On Sunday, strikes hit families in their homes. In Gaza City’s al-Sousi Tower, a strike killed Abdullah Abu Taif, 33, his pregnant wife, Abeer Anan, 29, and their five-year-old son, Azzam. Medics recovered the remains of an unborn child from the rubble, according to sources at al-Shifa Hospital.

In al-Qarara, near Khan Younis, a strike on an apartment killed Mahmoud al-Hams, 38, his wife, Fatima, 37, and their young daughter. Three others were wounded, medics at Nasser Hospital said.

Near Deir el-Balah, an elderly couple, Kamal and Huda Abu Muailiq, 68 and 59, were also killed in their home. A separate strike killed two brothers riding a motorbike in the same area.

Later that evening, a strike on a tent sheltering displaced people in Gaza City’s Remal neighbourhood killed two people, including a child. Four more people died in the neighbourhood when a drone struck a vehicle near the Sharia Court. Israel claimed the attack hit military operatives.

On Saturday, an overnight strike destroyed the medicine warehouse attached to Al-Aqsa Hospital in Deir el-Balah, wiping out two of four storage facilities and severely damaging two more. The Israeli military said it hit a Hamas weapons depot located next to the hospital, one of five such sites it said it struck that night.

Gaza Minister of Health Director-General Munir al-Bursh told Al Jazeera the strike “turns medicine and illness itself into a tool of war”.

The Health Ministry said that July was the deadliest month in Gaza since the start of the year, with 152 people killed. By August 3, the cumulative toll since the October 2025 “ceasefire” had reached 1,250 killed and more than 4,100 wounded.

On August 1, Gaza’s Civil Defence completed a two-week search of a flattened home in the Sabra neighbourhood, retrieving 112 bodies, 40 of them children. Some 157 people remained missing, according to Mohammed Abu Dan, who oversaw the recovery. Some, he said, were fused into concrete by the force of the explosions.

Thousands of bodies are believed to still be under the rubble across Gaza.

Elsewhere in Gaza this week, one-year-old Zaid Nofal was killed when a strike hit his family’s home in the Bureij refugee camp. In Khan Younis, an Israeli drone strike on a tent killed eight-year-old Ratil Abdullah and 20-year-old Abdullah al-Balawi, according to Gaza Now.

Israeli forces also further expanded the “Yellow Line”, which demarcates Israeli-occupied Gaza from the rest of the besieged territory, placing new concrete barriers on Salah al-Din Street – Gaza’s main north-south route – near Shujayea, cutting off displaced families from one of the Strip’s few remaining unobstructed roads.

The West Bank saw its own week of escalation, one that the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said made July, jointly with March, the deadliest month for Palestinians in incidents involving settlers since October 2023.

OCHA recorded more than 1,380 settler-related incidents across the West Bank since the start of 2026, averaging 6.6 a day. Demolitions and settler violence displaced an average of 17 people a day this year, double the rate of the previous three years.

A report released this week by the Palestinian National Bureau for Defending Land and Resisting Colonization said no soldier from Israel’s settler-heavy “Hagmar” defence units has been arrested for killing a Palestinian since at least 2017, and more than 93 percent of investigation files into settler attacks have been closed without indictment.

A week after four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed in Tal in the Nablus area, settlers walked through the village, escorted by Israeli soldiers and armoured vehicles. The same wave of settler encroachments saw a 10-year-old boy shot in the back on July 31 near al-Mughayyir. Israeli police subsequently arrested an off-duty soldier, a settler, on suspicion of the shooting, Haaretz reported.

Days later, settlers attacked Issam Radwan, 71, and his wife Nahil, 65, on their farmland near Beitillu, beating them with clubs. The village council head said Nahil suffered a fractured skull, a bite wound and a broken forearm, while Issam had a broken shin.

In Idhna, west of Hebron, armed settlers descended from a nearby outpost and attacked a Palestinian home. Soldiers who arrived later attacked residents who came to the family’s aid and fired tear gas at them.

As attacks and raids unfolded across the West Bank throughout the week, settlers erected new illegal outposts. While closures across the West Bank eased somewhat from the previous week’s near-total siege, the small town of Sinjil, north of Ramallah, and its roughly 8,000 residents entered a third week under closure. Its main entrance is still sealed with earth mounds and metal barriers, making routine trips difficult and potentially deadly.

Land seizures kept pace with the violence. In the Jenin governorate, Israeli authorities issued orders within days seizing roughly 200 dunums (0.2 square kilometres) of land, some of it for military roads stretching more than 11km to serve a network of outposts approved by the government, the Wafa news agency reported.

In the northern West Bank, Israeli NGO Kerem Navot documented what researcher Dror Etkes told Haaretz was an unprecedented step: military orders seizing Palestinian Authority-administered land in Area A – not for security, but to connect two new illegal settlements, Noa and Emek Dotan, ahead of Israeli families moving in next month.

In Masafer Yatta, an Israeli court rejected petitions against the demolition of the Zif secondary girls’ school, which serves 251 students, and three homes in Khirbet al-Mafqara, clearing the way for both to be razed at any time, Wafa and local activist Osama Makhamreh reported.

Adding to a steady stream of international criticism, Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry, said the settlements were “illegal under international law”. Israeli officials responded to the criticism by accusing Ottawa of moving to “embolden terror”.

The UN’s rights office, meanwhile, said it was “alarmed” by Israeli plans to expand settlements further.

title: Three lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan swelters
excerpt:
Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer

Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson s...
body_text:
Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer

Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, as the big cats struggle in Japan’s high levels of humidity.

Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new “cruelly hot day” designation.

Since mid-July, 10 of the 16 lions in Tama zoological park have suffered from “loss of appetite and decreased activity”, and three lionesses had died, the zoo said in a statement. One lioness died on Tuesday, another Friday, and the third on Sunday, it said.

The cause of the deaths is suspected to be heatstroke, as dehydration and multiple organ failure were observed by a veterinarian, the zoo said.

“Even though lions are thought to be resistant to heat, zoo keepers have been strengthening countermeasures to cope with Japan’s summer heat in recent years. Heat here comes with high humidity; that is different from heat with dry air in Africa,” a zoo spokesperson said.

“But this summer, heat arrived suddenly after the rainy season was over” in late July, they added.

“We are strengthening measures against the heat, sprinkling water, improving ventilation and installing spot air conditioners.”

The zoo said several lions are still being treated.

About 18,600 people in Japan were taken to hospital for heatstroke between 20 and 26 July, with 45 of them pronounced dead on arrival, according to the fire and disaster management agency.

Authorities have adjusted the timings of a string of cultural and sporting events in recent years because of the heat, including the World Cosplay Summit in Nagoya, which held its last summer edition last weekend.

Japan experiences about 1,300 heat-related deaths annually and is aiming to halve that number by 2030. The country’s highest recorded temperature was registered in August last year: 41.8C in Isesaki, north of Tokyo.

Scientists say human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat events in Japan and elsewhere. South Korea is currently engulfed by a heatwave, with the rising summer temperatures linked to at least 16 deaths.

title: Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years
excerpt:
Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour

A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because...
body_text:
Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour

A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed in New Zealand, ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations.

The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host of kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island.

“We don’t take for granted that we’ve had this success because it had us baffled for so long,” said Andy Mentor, the project manager for Pest Free Purerua, a conservation project.

New Zealand has one of the highest rates of cat ownership in the world, and the impact of feral and domestic cats on biodiversity ignites fierce debate. Some on social media were horrified Nine Lives had been shot, believing it deserved to live, while others said its capture was “a fantastic result”.

Nine Lives will form part of that debate long after its death, with its body set to be taxidermied for use as a tool to educate the community about the devastating impact of feral cats on native species.

Nine Lives was first spotted on the Purerua peninsula in Northland in 2023. What ensued was a frustrating and twisted game of cat and mouse.

Pest Free Purerua had just introduced 20 pāteke, or brown teal – the country’s rarest mainland duck – to the peninsula, believing it had control over the feral cat population.

“But within a week we had our first death. We put up some cameras and we identified a particular cat with specific markings,” Mentor said. Another 15 pāteke were killed, with the same cat turning up.

“It was a really stressful time. So we brought in more traps, gear, night cameras to try and get to the root cause of the problem.”

The project managed to catch other feral cats over the next year, but Nine Lives remained elusive. They decided to release more pāteke in 2024 but the same cat appeared, killing another 15 of the 20 birds.

“This particular cat would be very erratic. It would show up in a particular place and then not show up for another two or three months. It would show up in the dusk, midnight, early morning, through the day, so it was never a predictable pattern, which made it very, very difficult to track,” Mentor said.

The team came close to catching it on a number of occasions, but each time it slipped their grasp, earning it the name Nine Lives.

At the end of July, Mentor and his team noticed the cat had turned up to a quarry three nights in a row, which was “quite unusual”. They laid out salmon, fried chicken and rabbit to attract the animal, and deployed cages and traps.

On 30 July, a notification on a cellphone camera showed a cat in one of the cages.

“We dispatched our trappers to check it out and there it was. So it was humanely shot,” Mentor said.

The animal will have its stomach contents examined to see what it was feeding on before being taxidermied. Mentor said it has likely also fed on kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife.

More than 2.5m feral cats roam New Zealand’s bush and on offshore islands, where they can grow up to a metre long, including their tail. They have destroyed native wildlife and hunted some bird species to the brink of extinction.

In November, the government announced feral cats would be added to the country’s world-leading Predator-Free 2050 strategy. Mentor said moving from the suppression of cats to an elimination strategy will be a “real step up” for the peninsula and the team may restart introducing pāteke once more.

But for now, conservationists will celebrate the capture of Nine Lives, as well as honour their most evasive adversary. “Nine Lives needs to be given a certain amount of dignity and respect,” said Mentor.

title: Tuesday briefing: Inside the right’s heated climate-denial debate
excerpt:
In today’s newsletter: A small chorus of right-leaning critics are trying to convince politicians that climate action is deeply unpopular, downplaying its seriousness in the process

Good morning. Hal...
body_text:
In today’s newsletter: A small chorus of right-leaning critics are trying to convince politicians that climate action is deeply unpopular, downplaying its seriousness in the process

Good morning. Half of England and all of Wales are officially in drought, wildfires have burned through parts of the Cairngorms, Suffolk and the Isle of Wight, and reservoirs are running low. Farmers have warned that there could soon be food shortages, and the Royal Horticultural Society is considering moving its hydrangeas to cope with the heat. Many people are now asking a question rarely associated with British summertime: when will it rain?

The Guardian has been covering how the climate crisis is supercharging wildfires in Europe, the impossible choices firefighters face about which places to save, the number of people who have died in England due to heat, and the air conditioning haves and have-nots. Had you been reading another newspaper, you may have come away with a very different impression of this extreme weather.

Over the last week, a string of articles, mostly in the Telegraph, suggested that Britain should give up on net zero and learn to live with its newly Mediterranean climate; that wildfires had been exacerbated by environmental groups; and, rather grandiosely, that climate “catastrophism” is a “leftist weapon” designed to “destroy capitalism”.

In a week when England entered its fourth heatwave of 2026, this line of argument might have seemed more than a little out of touch. But it reflects how climate deniers are reconfiguring their narratives in the face of an indisputable crisis. I spoke to Bob Ward, policy and communications director at the Grantham Research Institute on Climate Change, about how a minority is shaping the political debate and trying to thwart the transition, even while most people want to see more action on climate. First, here are the headlines.

UK news | Rapists, child sexual abusers and groomers will be excluded from early release plans to ease critical prison overcrowding in a major intervention by Andy Burnham.

UK politics | Nigel Farage has made his clearest admission that he was in talks to return to lead Reform UK months before the 2024 general election, casting fresh doubt on previous claims that he was not involved in politics when he received a £5m gift.

Spain | A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.

Middle East | New talks between Washington and Tehran are the “last chance” for Iran to forge a deal and avoid an escalation of US strikes on the country, Donald Trump said on Monday.

Environment | A plastic manufacturer in the north of England is facing potential legal action over emissions of benzene, a carcinogenic chemical with no safe level, the Guardian can reveal.

As the world heats up, denying the reality of climate change has become implausible. “This is no longer a matter of speculation: the wildfires of Europe, pitiless and persistent, are the way we live now,” the Telegraph’s Tim Stanley wrote recently in an article persuading the right to “get serious” about the subject.

Instead, a tendency to downplay the seriousness of the crisis has emerged. In this week’s issue of the Spectator, Matt Ridley, a former Conservative peer whose ancestral estate features two coalmines, suggested that a “cult of rewilding” – whose converts allegedly include the RSPB and National Trust – is connected to the risk of wildfires in England (this suggestion was repeated in another Spectator piece on Saturday, £). The Spanish far-right party Vox recently made a similar argument about wildfires in Spain, blaming them on a failure to clear rural areas and invest in firefighting services, rather than on the climate crisis (read Sam Jones’s piece on Spain’s climate deniers here).

Another line of argument is to acknowledge that the climate crisis is real, but insist that nothing can be done to address it. “The war against global warming has been lost, with only grievous collateral damage to show for it,” Allister Heath, the Sunday editor of the Telegraph, wrote last week (£) in a piece arguing that people in Britain should learn to love their new Mediterranean climate, and take inspiration from other “blossoming” hot regions, such as Dubai and Israel.

“All of this commentary reflects a battle on the right between climate sceptics – people often referred to as ‘lukewarmers’ – versus the Conservative voters who actually care about conservation, nature and so on,” Ward told me. The term “lukewarmer” was popularised by Ridley, who is affiliated with the Global Warming Policy Foundation, a campaigning body that has spent decades undermining climate science, and its campaigning arm, Net Zero Watch. “Lukewarmers accept the reality of human-made climate change, but believe the impact of it won’t be as big as people argue, and that policies involved in mitigating these impacts will be expensive and difficult,” Ward says.

Net zero has become a particular focus for them. Basic physics dictates that reaching net zero is necessary to stop global temperatures rising even further. Although it was Theresa May, a Tory, who committed Britain to reaching net zero emissions by 2050, voices in the rightwing press have sought to paint the target as a bureaucratic conspiracy devised by lanyard-toting Labour wonks and enforced on an unsuspecting population, spreading “desolation across the loveliest countryside in the world”, as one writer recently put it (£).

If Britain doesn’t  contribute that much to global emissions, does net zero even matter?

Another common refrain (I counted at least five articles about the climate crisis published in the Telegraph last week that made variations of this argument) is that, since other countries emit far more carbon than Britain, striving for net zero in the UK is, at best, an irrelevance and, at worst, a decision that will make the country much poorer than other industrialising nations. As the “anti-woke” libertarian podcaster Konstantin Kisin said in a speech to the Oxford Union in 2023, the future of climate change will be decided by “poor people in Asia and Latin America who could not give a crap about saving the planet … because they are poor”.

People who make this argument often point to China, which produces about 35% of global carbon dioxide emissions. Since the UK produces less than 1%, why should the UK bother decarbonising when it’s not even responsible for that much damage? “That’s a totally daft argument,” says Ward. “If more than 99% of the emissions damaging the UK come from other countries, then we have a vested interest in persuading those countries to accelerate their transition. And we’re not going to persuade them by dragging our feet.”

In fact, China has massively expanded its renewables sector, and has a far higher proportion of electric cars on the road than in Britain. Meanwhile, commentators in Britain are trying to forestall the transition by making misleading arguments about China.

The 2024 Conservative manifesto committed to reaching net zero by 2050, but Kemi Badenoch ditched the target, perhaps hoping to win back Reform voters (a month before U-turning on the pledge, Badenoch spent a week on a “retreat” hosted by the Tory donor and chair of Net Zero Watch). And among the reported reasons why Ed Miliband didn’t get the role of chancellor were his commitment to net zero and his opposition to new exploration licences in the North Sea.

Most British voters are in favour of net zero. Despite this, media coverage of it is more than twice as likely to be negative than positive. This could be helping to drive a false perception that climate action is overwhelmingly unpopular with voters, encouraging MPs to significantly underestimate public support for these policies, and overestimate opposition.

In other words, a small chorus of climate sceptics aren’t trying to represent public opinion or persuade us to embrace Mediterranean summers, so much as convince politicians that climate action is deeply unpopular.

For more on extreme weather and the climate crisis, sign up to our free (and very good) weekly email Down to Earth. Click here to subscribe. It features an exclusive weekly piece from our top climate crisis correspondents, as well as a digest of the biggest environment stories.

I’ve had a sneak peek at the Guardian’s new This Is India newsletter, which launches this morning (you’ll be able to read it online imminently), and Niha Masih’s dispatch from the frontline of the Cockroach movement is essential reading. Sign up for This Is India here to read future editions first. Sam Coare, newsletters team

I have fond memories of visiting Blockbuster and arguing with my brother over which VHS our parents would rent us for the weekend, so I loved this piece about the lost civic life of video rental shops. Hettie

Audacious when they come off, humiliating when they don’t … this celebration of 50 years of the Panenka shows how thin the line is between footballing genius and stupidity. Sam

It’s worth listening to this morning’s episode of Today in Focus with Anna Isaac about her latest story on Nigel Farage’s funding scandals. Her reporting on this has been unmissable. Hettie

The Guardian’s annual invertebrate of the year competition is back! Can the reigning champion Milnesium tardigradum defend its spineless crown? The reveal of the 10-strong shortlist is under way, with today’s spotlight turning on the common woodlouse. Sam

Tour de France Femmes | Sigrid Haugset, the Norwegian national champion, shocked the established order in the Tour de France Femmes by breaking away to take the overall lead.

Fifa | The English FA and Serbia’s have followed Wales’s and Finland’s in dropping support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election bid as Fifa president.

Tennis | Emma Raducanu will miss the US Open because of the stress fracture in her right leg that she sustained during the grass-court season and forced her to pull out of Wimbledon.

“Rapists and groomers will not be freed early, says PM”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the Telegraph writes “Pc Harper killers will still be freed early” and the Times says “Killers but not rapists to be given early release”.

The Mail has “Athens suitcase murder suspect”, the i Paper leads on “Driest July in 190 years”, the FT leads on “Apple launches legal challenge to new demand for data access”, and the Mirror splashes “Farage’s sinking ship”.

Elsewhere, the Express goes with “Two jabs a year to target ‘silent killer’” and Metro has “15st lighter … and jabs are just the job”.

How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe

Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The incident has led to a political crisis in Spain and criticism from EU countries.

Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam – watch on YouTube.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

When she was a teenager, Amy Annette spent summers wrapped up in a black cardigan and was often asked: “Aren’t you hot in that?” She wasn’t hiding from the heat, but from years of feeling ashamed and insecure about her arms. Last month, after decades of avoiding sleeveless tops, the heatwave pushed Annette to bare her arms in public for the first time, at 37 – prompting her to rethink the body standards that had shaped her wardrobe, and her confidence, for decades. “And if it gets any hotter,” she says, “I’m wondering what other internalised standards I can sweat out.”

Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

title: Pennsylvania school bus aide accused of sexually assaulting special needs teen
excerpt: The father of the Georgia school shooter, Colin Gray, is sentenced to 15 years in prison. Legal analyst Donna Rotunno joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the historic sentencing precedent and paren...
body_text:
The father of the Georgia school shooter, Colin Gray, is sentenced to 15 years in prison. Legal analyst Donna Rotunno joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the historic sentencing precedent and parental responsibility.

A Pennsylvania school bus aide was arrested after he allegedly inappropriately touched a 14-year-old girl with special needs and appeared to take photographs and videos of her with his cellphone, according to police.

Ali Khan, 62, was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors, indecent assault and related offenses, the Bensalem Township Police Department said.

Khan was being held at the Bucks County Correctional Facility after failing to post 10% of his $500,000 bail.

The girl’s parents contacted police on Thursday, July 30, to report that their daughter had allegedly been inappropriately touched by a bus aide earlier that day, according to investigators.

HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP

Ali Khan, 62, was arrested for inappropriately touching a special needs teenager. (Bensalem Township Police)

Police said their investigation determined that Khan allegedly touched the Bensalem High School student multiple times on Wednesday, July 29, and Thursday, July 30, while she was riding a bus to the school’s extended school year program.

Investigators said surveillance footage from inside the bus showed Khan directing the girl to a specific seat before allegedly touching her inappropriately while securing her seatbelt and after she was seated.

Police said the footage also appeared to show Khan engaging in sexual conduct and using a cellphone to photograph or record the girl.

Ali Khan was charged with endangering the welfare of a child, corruption of minors and indecent assault. (Google Maps)

"Bensalem Police would like to commend the victim of this assault for having the courage to come forward and report the assault," police said. "Additionally, Bensalem Police would like to thank the Bensalem School District for their assistance with this investigation. The safety and well-being of our students continues to be the top priority of both the Bensalem Township Police Department and the Bensalem School District."

The Bensalem Township School District said the employee was immediately removed from service and from the district pending the outcome of criminal and administrative investigations.

"The safety and well-being of our students is our highest priority," the district said in a statement. "Whenever concerns involving student safety are brought to our attention, we act immediately to protect students, support families, and cooperate fully with law enforcement. We are committed to conducting a thorough administrative review while respecting the integrity of the criminal investigation."

CALIFORNIA MIDDLE SCHOOL ASSISTANT PRINCIPAL NABBED IN CHILD SEX STING

The footage showed Ali Khan putting his hand inside his pants and touching himself during the encounter. (Bensalem Township Police)

"The district is fully cooperating with the Bensalem Township Police Department and will continue to assist law enforcement as requested. The district will also continue its own administrative investigation in accordance with Board policy, district procedures, and applicable law," the statement added.

Khan’s preliminary hearing is scheduled for Aug. 11, 2026.

The incident remains under investigation.

title: Public urged to avoid hospital unless ‘life might be in danger’ after record day for Sydney emergency departments
excerpt:
Winter flu season is putting pressure on the health system, with medical staff bracing for the ‘worst three weeks of the year’

Sick patients in New South Wales have been told to avoid the emergency r...
body_text:
Winter flu season is putting pressure on the health system, with medical staff bracing for the ‘worst three weeks of the year’

Sick patients in New South Wales have been told to avoid the emergency room unless their life is at risk after a record day for winter presentations put the hospital system under strain.

The New South Wales health minister, Ryan Park, said just under 10,000 people presented to emergency departments in Sydney on Monday, the “biggest ever recorded winter day in history”. It was around 1,000 more people than the average.

“That is a demonstration of the sort of pressure our staff in the health system are under right now,” he said, adding west and south-west Sydney had been the hardest hit.

There were also 4,100 ambulance callouts, which was “far more” than predicted, Park said. On Tuesday, the state government announced a permanent command centre to coordinate peak hospital demands this winter, working with the 17 local health districts and NSW ambulance to redirect patients away from EDs with high numbers of presentations.

Park said operational hours would also be extended for some hospital services later in the day and for weekends.

“We know that we are in the middle of winter, and that is what we are likely to see over the next few weeks: ongoing presentations around influenza, Covid, and RSV,” he said. “There is no need to go to an emergency department unless it is an emergency.”

Instead, Park urged people to use Healthdirect, a phone service that connects users to registered nurses for advice and referrals, or urgent care services, which typically operate from 8am until 8pm. He said the government was looking at whether this could be extended.

The latest respiratory surveillance report from NSW Health, for the week ending 25 July, found influenza and RSV was at a “moderate level” and Covid-19 was at a “low level”. ED presentations for influenza were hovering at around 400, well below a peak of more than 1,000 in July 2025 but an increase on recent weeks. There were 2,509 notified cases of influenza in the same time period, which health authorities expected would grow.

Park told ABC Radio Sydney that the situation had been exacerbated by vaccine hesitancy. He said there had been a challenge in encouraging uptake of the influenza vaccination ahead of winter, which costs $15 unless you are under five, over 64 or vulnerable.

“We have had vaccine hesitancy off the back of Covid … and this is what health systems are dealing with, not just in our country, but around the world,” he said. “We need to change that.”

Park also took aim at the NDIS, claiming there were 1,300 people “stuck in our state’s hospitals who are age care or NDIS [patients]”.

“I spoke to an emergency director this morning from Westmead … and they said … one of the frustrations is trying to get people … out of those beds, and back into the community,” he said.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, told 2GB the state’s emergency health services were bracing for the “worst three weeks of the year”.

“The cold weather’s really set in now. And I’ve spoken to emergency departments in Maitland, in Cessnock, in Western Sydney … who have said it’s a late starting season, but it’s hitting us hard now,” he said.

“To the extent that you can go to an urgent care clinic or see your GP … If it’s not life-threatening, we genuinely suggest that you do that, so the doctors can focus and nurses can focus their efforts and attention on people that are about to die.”

He said resuscitation bays, located immediately behind emergency department waiting rooms, were “all occupied”.

“If you feel or you’ve got any suspicion that your life might be in danger, please go to the emergency department, please call 000.”

An ED nurse at a major metropolitan Sydney hospital, who wished to remain anonymous, said it had been “extremely busy” on Monday, with wait times of up to 10 hours. She urged people who weren’t experiencing a severe emergency to visit urgent care clinics, but said the issue was “people don’t know it’s available”.

“Work needs to be done with GPs and primary health networks on what their responsibility is,” she said. “We aren’t an outpatient clinic.”

National data from the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare shows urgent and semi-urgent cases account for the vast majority of presentations at EDS.

Minns claimed part of the problem was a historical “underinvestment” in health infrastructure, particularly in Western Sydney. “We’ve done a massive redevelopment of Westmead [Hospital], but the pressures are real,” he said.

The latest data from the Bureau of Health Information (BHI) found there were 791,987 ED attendees in NSW hospitals from January to March, up 0.9% compared with the same quarter the previous year.

The leader of the opposition, Kellie Sloane, said it was a “shocking state of affairs” to have the government telling people not to go to emergency departments “unless you absolutely have to”.

The president of the NSW Australian Medical Association, Dr Fred Betros, said it wasn’t an “unforeseen crisis”.

“Telling patients to stay away from emergency departments is not a health strategy,” he said. “NSW needs more consultant doctors, properly staffed beds, modern industrial arrangements … and serious investment in prevention, general practice and public outpatient care.”

title: Why are the Washington wildfires so severe? Spokane fires explained
excerpt:
Wildfires in Washington State force tens of thousands to flee

A cluster of fast-moving wildfires has devastated the outskirts of Spokane, Washington state, with 65,000 people told to leave their home...
body_text:
Wildfires in Washington State force tens of thousands to flee

A cluster of fast-moving wildfires has devastated the outskirts of Spokane, Washington state, with 65,000 people told to leave their homes. More than 700 buildings have been destroyed as the fires spread from surrounding vegetation into residential neighbourhoods, posing an unprecedented threat to lives and property.

The blazes have become the top firefighting priority in the US because of their scale and the danger they pose to communities. While no deaths have been confirmed, authorities say it will take time to assess the full extent of the damage as search teams begin entering the hardest-hit areas.

The evacuation orders expanded from about 4,000 people on Sunday to 65,000 by Monday, highlighting the speed at which the fires spread into populated communities.

Spokane, Washington’s second-largest city, is at the centre of one of the state’s most destructive wildfire emergencies in recent history after three fast-moving wildfires erupted on its northern outskirts over the weekend. Fanned by strong winds and fueled by exceptionally dry vegetation, the fires have burned more than 8,000 acres (3237 hectares) and spread from surrounding forests and grasslands into residential neighbourhoods, forcing approximately 65,000 people to evacuate, according to the Spokane Valley Fire Department.

Hundreds of buildings, most of them homes, have already been destroyed, with aerial surveys suggesting many more may have been damaged. Entire neighbourhoods have been reduced to charred rubble, with some properties left standing only as brick chimneys.

The scale of the disaster has overwhelmed local resources, prompting one of the largest firefighting operations in the state, with more than 1,000 firefighters deployed from across the region.

Despite the massive response, the fires remain uncontained, and officials say it could take days to fully assess the destruction. While no deaths have been confirmed, authorities initially received nearly 300 reports of missing people after the evacuations, though that number has since fallen significantly as families have been reunited. Emergency shelters have been opened across Spokane, and officials are urging residents not to return to evacuated areas or fly drones, which can disrupt critical aerial firefighting operations.

Firefighters are taking advantage of a brief period of cooler temperatures and lighter winds, but forecasters warn that hotter, drier and windier weather is expected to return later this week, raising fears that the fires could spread even further.

Washington is experiencing one of its worst wildfire seasons in more than three decades, with about 450,000 acres (182,000 hectares) burned so far this summer. More than 250,000 acres have burned in recent major fires alone.

Local news outlets have reported that the Spokane County Sheriff’s Office announced on Monday evening that a 37-year-old had been arrested on suspicion of arson in connection with the fire.

However, experts say the conditions that allowed the fires to spread so rapidly were already in place.

Washington has been experiencing severe drought and an unusually low winter snowpack, leaving vegetation exceptionally dry and highly flammable. Those conditions have been compounded by periods of extreme heat, low humidity and strong winds, creating an environment in which even a small ignition can quickly grow into a fast-moving wildfire.

Scientists have also linked increasingly severe wildfire seasons across the western US to human-caused climate change, which has contributed to hotter temperatures, longer droughts and drier landscapes. While climate change does not directly ignite wildfires, it makes them more likely to spread rapidly and become more destructive once they start.

The Washington wildfires have become particularly severe because several factors have converged, allowing the blazes to spread rapidly.

Scientists say drought, extreme heat and climate change are making wildfire seasons longer, more frequent and more destructive across the western US.

Drought dries out vegetation, turning forests and grasslands into fuel that can ignite and burn more intensely.

Heat and low humidity accelerate fire spread by drying vegetation even further and creating conditions in which flames can move rapidly across the landscape.

Climate change amplifies these conditions, as rising global temperatures are increasing the likelihood of prolonged droughts, more frequent heatwaves and longer fire seasons, making large, destructive wildfires more likely once they ignite.

The weather is expected to worsen again by midweek.

While Monday and Tuesday offered a brief, helpful window of cooler temperatures and calmer winds, the midweek forecast calls for a return of:

Because the fires remain completely uncontained, authorities are keeping evacuations in place. They warn that the worst outcome would be letting residents return to their homes, only to have to evacuate them again 24 to 48 hours later when the hot, windy weather returns.

Washington’s entire congressional delegation is awaiting a response from President Donald Trump regarding their request for an expedited emergency declaration to deliver immediate federal relief to displaced families.

According to the National Interagency Fire Center, most of the fire activity in the US remains concentrated across the country’s northwest.

Right now, the major fires are mostly grassland burns in Idaho, Oregon and Utah, as well as fires in Florida’s Everglades National Park, in addition to new fires reported in Left Creek in Wyoming, Antelope Creek Fire in Nevada and the Sand Creek and Middle Coulee fires in Montana.

A lightning-caused fire that has burned more than 530 square miles (about 1,370 sq km) of grassland in western Idaho and eastern Oregon continued to grow on Monday. The area is home to cattle ranches, and authorities said the fire is threatening more than 600 homes and 800 other structures.

In central Utah, a blaze quadrupled in size more than the weekend to nearly 109 square miles (282 sq km) by Monday afternoon. More than 100 cattle have died, according to law enforcement.

title: Cancer survivors need protection from future discrimination, say German politicians
excerpt:
Campaigners say people who have had cancer face discrimination in areas including bank loans, adoption of children and insurance

German politicians who have survived cancer have spearheaded proposals...
body_text:
Campaigners say people who have had cancer face discrimination in areas including bank loans, adoption of children and insurance

German politicians who have survived cancer have spearheaded proposals to protect people long in remission from what they call rampant discrimination in areas including bank loans, adoption of children and insurance.

The policy known as “the right to be forgotten” (RTBF) is a central demand of a community estimated to number 5.5 million people in Germany: former cancer patients who have been given a clean bill of health by their doctors.

“Anyone who has medically overcome cancer must not be permanently disadvantaged in any area of life, be it in insurance, credit or employment law,” reads the proposed measure drawn up by the Social Democrats (SPD), junior partners in Germany’s coalition government.

Once medically justified time limits – generally five years – have expired, “disclosure of a previously overcome cancer diagnosis can no longer be required”, the paper states.

One of the proposal’s initiators is Adis Ahmetović, the foreign policy spokesperson of the SPD’s parliamentary group, who went public with a lymphoma diagnosis at the age of 30 and is now 33. He has been tumour-free since October 2024 and could be medically considered cancer-free in 2029.

Ahmetović argues that beyond its ethical justification, the policy “would not cost the state a cent”.

He received support from his fellow Social Democrat Manuela Schwesig, who is a breast cancer survivor and the state premier of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on the Baltic coast.

Schwesig said Germany remained among EU outliers in creating high obstacles to a fresh start for former cancer patients.

“You have the right [in other countries] to make plans again as normal: to buy a house, to start a family,” she told the Funke media group. “Other European countries have long since sorted this out. We need a law for this; voluntary commitments are not enough.”

The SPD’s co-leader Lars Klingbeil, who is Germany’s finance minister, overcame tongue cancer, after learning of his illness in 2014. He has also thrown his weight behind the legislation.

“Anyone who has beaten cancer must be able to look ahead freely again, socially and economically,” he said.

A petition calling for Germany to adopt RTBF reforms has drawn more than 55,000 signatures. It was initiated by Tobias Burggraf, whose daughter was diagnosed with cancer at the age of two and a half.

“After the healing, life begins – not the next hurdle,” Burggraf said, describing his goal. He said the SPD-sponsored proposal “covers the thrust of our petition”, calling it “correct and long overdue”.

The SPD parliamentary group cited survey data from a patients’ rights lobbying group showing that 77% of medically declared cancer survivors face what it called discrimination when taking out private insurance policies.

However, the German Insurance Association (GDV), an industry group, warned against setting fixed time limits on cancer patient status. It said private insurance providers of life and disability coverage must be able to assess patients’ future risk based on scientific review and medical advice to keep policies affordable for all.

“Even after successful treatment, relapses, long-term effects of the therapy or lasting health problems may persist,” said the association’s general manager, Jörg Asmussen. “There may also be an increased risk of other diseases, particularly other types of cancer.”

Susanne Weg-Remers, of the German Cancer Research Centre in the western city of Heidelberg, said that while some cancer survivors did develop tumours in other organs, the risk was not significantly higher than in the general population.

Given that one in two men and one in two to three women in Germany will develop a malignant tumour at some point in their lives, “if you were to use cancer as an argument,” she told Süddeutsche newspaper, “you wouldn’t be allowed to sell insurance policies or grant loans at all”.

Patient advocacy groups say automatic presumptions about future health are particularly unfair to younger survivors, whose prognoses are often good.

The German Foundation for Young Adults with Cancer said 16,500 people aged 18 to 39 were diagnosed with cancer in Germany each year, as well as 2,100 children, but medical advances meant more than 80% of the two groups could be healed.

The European Society for Medical Oncology, which provides cancer information and education, has advocated for a fair common standard for financial services access for cancer survivors across Europe based on a five-year minimum remission period. The society said the current patchwork of laws across the EU led to “unjustified discrimination”.

Only 11 EU member states had introduced specific legal measures protecting cancer survivors from financial discrimination, it said, leaving 16 without equivalent protections. “As a result, access to financial services continues to depend heavily on where a cancer survivor lives.”

An EU directive that Germany is still working to implement allows for restrictions for a period of up to 15 years after the end of treatment and offers narrow protections in the context of credit and insurance.

The UK has no binding RTBF laws. While Ireland passed such a law in 2026 focused on a level playing field for mortgage seekers, the UK has a largely voluntary framework.

title: Approval of east London datacentre labelled ‘slap in the face’ for local democracy
excerpt:
Campaigners decry Angela Rayner’s backing for Brick Lane project that has only 11 affordable homes

A £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery estate in Brick Lane, east London, has been approved, cl...
body_text:
Campaigners decry Angela Rayner’s backing for Brick Lane project that has only 11 affordable homes

A £500m redevelopment of the Truman Brewery estate in Brick Lane, east London, has been approved, clearing the way for the construction of a datacentre, offices and apartments despite opposition from Tower Hamlets council and local campaign groups.

The housing secretary, Angela Rayner, made the decision in a letter issued on her behalf last week by the housing minister Matthew Pennycook, rejecting demands from the council and campaigners for for the site to be used for hundreds of homes instead.

The Save Brick Lane coalition, made up of nine groups opposed to the project, said their “community should not be expected to accept a noisy, energy-intensive development that consumes a significant amount of power”.

Dr Fatima Rajina of Nijjor Manush, one of the groups in the coalition, said it “will cause people who have lived in the area to move out, which will break up families. The people who made Brick Lane what it is will be seen as artefacts”.

She said the group had asked the local community “what they want and what Brick Lane means to them”, and that many people had said they simply wanted their families to stay together.

The property owners, Truman Estates and Zeloof LLP, propose six new blocks, a datacentre, offices and 44 homes. It will also include a cinema, exhibition and events space, art galleries, shops, cafes, restaurants, community spaces, a food market and workspace.

Rajina said campaigners had worked with architects, policymakers and planners, who had come up with a master plan that Tower Hamlets adopted in September 2024 that would have created 350 homes.

That was overturned by the government’s decision. Pennycook’s letter said there was “no detailed evidence” of the feasibility and deliverability of an alternative, housing-centred scheme, and rejected demands for it.

The Tower Hamlets mayor, Lutfur Rahman, said the decision was “deeply disappointing and a missed opportunity to deliver the social and affordable housing that … residents urgently need”.

Rajina described the overturning of the council’s unanimous decision as the “trumping” of local democracy and said it felt like a slap in the face.

Pennycook’s letter said the datacentre’s scale “would relate in a reasonable way to the other buildings in the vicinity” and that the wider proposals would “very clearly enhance both the character and appearance of the Brick Lane and Fournier Street conservation area”.

The letter specifically addressed concerns raised by the area’s Bangladeshi community, noting that the six social rented homes had been designed to meet local housing needs, including for larger families with Bangladeshi heritage.

Rajina criticised the government’s approach. “It’s frustrating when hearing about Andy Burnham and Angela Rayner creating a new language around localism, but giving so much power to landlords, directly pushing out locals,” she said.

She also raised concerns about the datacentre’s water use. It “will use a huge amount of water and local people will suffer, water will become a luxury commodity”, she said.

One person who works in the area said: “We don’t need it … Brick Lane is the heart of community, there’s already been so much change and adding a datacentre will just be another bad change.”

Of the 44 homes to be built, 11 will be affordable and six will be designated as social homes available to rent. More than 30,000 households are registered as awaiting social housing in Tower Hamlets.

The Save Brick Lane coalition is seeking expert advice on whether Rayner’s decision can be challenged.

Truman Estates has been approached for comment.

title: GPs’ breast cancer guidelines ‘miss’ 95% of women who will develop disease
excerpt:
Findings prompt calls for review of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence criteria

Young women in England who later develop breast cancer are not being referred for early tests or prevent...
body_text:
Findings prompt calls for review of National Institute for Health and Care Excellence criteria

Young women in England who later develop breast cancer are not being referred for early tests or preventive treatment because current guidelines used by GPs miss 95% of patients, research suggests.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) criteria used to decide who should be referred by family doctors for further breast cancer risk assessment and specialist care is failing to spot the vast majority of women under 50 who will go on to develop the disease in the next 10 years, according to the University of Cambridge and the Institute of Cancer Research, London (ICR).

The findings, published in the British Journal of Cancer, prompted calls for a review of the criteria.

Breast cancer is the most common cancer worldwide. It accounts for about one in four cases of cancer and is one of the leading causes of death in women under 50. Identifying women at higher risk early can pave the way for additional screening or preventive treatment.

But the current criteria given to GPs in England to refer women at risk of breast cancer for further tests or specialist care miss up to 95% of patients under 50 who go on to develop the disease within a decade, the analysis suggests.

Spotting those at the highest risk earlier would give doctors a better chance at treating or even preventing breast cancer, experts said.

In England, women at a higher risk of the disease are referred by GPs for further assessment and specialist care. This is based on family history, as well as criteria set by Nice.

Comparing the current guidelines with a new risk assessment system developed by Cambridge and funded by Cancer Research UK, called Boadicea, experts identified eight times as many women in the age group who would develop breast cancer.

The researchers said the Nice criteria miss up to 95% of women aged under 50 with a higher-than-average risk of breast cancer, and 95% of women who go on to develop the disease within 10 years.

A major reason for the disparity is because almost three-quarters of women (73%) under 50 who develop breast cancer within 10 years have no family history of breast cancer, the key criteria in the Nice guidelines.

Boadicea also looked in detail at other factors such as reproductive history, lifestyle and genetics.

Dr Juliet Usher-Smith, of the University of Cambridge, said: “We need to get better at identifying women at highest risk of breast cancer so that we can intervene early, when there are more options for treating, or even preventing, their disease.

“The current Nice criteria used in general practice are missing up to 95% of women under 50 who will go on to develop breast cancer. It’s time to look again at these criteria in the light of our findings.”

Prof Montserrat García-Closas, of the ICR, said: “There will be a balance to strike: the Nice criteria are much easier to implement, but miss a large proportion of women at elevated risk. But a full risk assessment including genetic testing will place a heavy burden on resources.

“Ultimately, it will be a trade-off between the practical, resource, and cost implications of data collection and risk assessment, and the potential benefits and harms associated with accurate and inaccurate classification of women.”

Dr Simon Vincent, chief scientific officer at Breast Cancer Now, which supported the study, said new ways to identify women at increased risk could help prevent some breast cancers or detect them earlier, when treatment was more likely to be successful.

“These findings highlight the limitations of Nice’s current referral criteria, and so this research must now be carefully considered as part of the current review of its family history guidelines.

“However, it’s equally important that any changes come with the needed investment in family history services, so they can be implemented effectively and fairly across the NHS.”

A Nice spokesperson said: “Nice welcomes the findings of this study and recognises the potential of multifactorial risk models in improving the identification of women at increased risk of breast cancer in the future.

“However, the current evidence does not warrant a change to our existing familial breast cancer guideline at this time. Nice remains committed to reviewing new evidence and will consider further updates as more data on feasibility and clinical outcomes become available.”

title: UK plastic manufacturer could face legal action over toxic emissions
excerpt:
Exclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzene

A plastic manufacturer in the north of England is facing potential lega...
body_text:
Exclusive: Environment Agency is considering whether to prosecute Huntsman Polyurethanes over emissions of carcinogenic benzene

A plastic manufacturer in the north of England is facing potential legal action over emissions of benzene, a carcinogenic chemical with no safe level, the Guardian can reveal.

The Environment Agency (EA) is considering taking legal action against Huntsman Polyurethanes in Teesside for a potential breach of licence, which is a criminal offence.

Campaigners say it has shone a light on the toxic nature of the global plastics industry and that workers and the local community have been put at risk.

Huntsman Polyurethanes, a petrochemical company that manufactures chemicals to produce plastic, sits within the sprawling Teesside chemical cluster in the seaside town of Redcar, North Yorkshire. The factory is part of Huntsman Corporation, a publicly traded global producer and marketer of chemical products which boasted revenues of $6bn in 2025.

In 2023, Huntsman decommissioned a process that was reducing its benzene air emissions and replaced it with an alternative method controlled by a third party.

However, EA documents show this new process “periodically paused”, with benzene consequently emitted directly to the air. The documents also show the EA was aware of this problem in 2023, but did not investigate until this year.

During this time, the benzene emissions from the site rose from 13 tonnes in 2022 to 17 tonnes in 2024, according to EA records.

Benzene, which is used to make some plastics, is carcinogenic to humans and causes leukaemia. According to the World Health Organization there is no safe level of exposure.

In an inspection report from March, the EA recorded several permit breaches in relation to the benzene emissions. The document states benzene is a carcinogen and it is “reasonably foreseeable that the deficiencies in the management system will cause multiple emissions, that when agglomerated, may result in a significant impact on the environment or human health until resolved through compliance”.

Failure to comply with an environmental permit is a criminal offence.

A Huntsman spokesperson said the benzene emissions were not illegal and were “fully compliant with our permit conditions”.

However, the EA told the Guardian: “We are considering further enforcement action with our legal team in relation to these permit breaches and have informed the UK Health Security Agency and the Health and Safety Executive so that they can assess any public or occupational health risks”.

Huntsman was instructed by the EA to carry out modelling to assess the impact of the benzene emissions in March 2026. The modelling found “significant” breaches of air quality standards in all scenarios considered. These standards are legally binding and are set to protect human health from toxic pollutants. In one scenario, the benzene emissions were predicted to exceed the 24-hour limit by 933%.

However, the EA told the Guardian an internal review of the modelling found the impacts to be “not insignificant but predicted environmental concentrations remain below the relevant environmental standards”.

“Our air quality experts have assessed environmental and human health impacts – their feedback indicates that these emissions do not pose a significant risk to local sites such as nearby schools,” the spokesperson added.

However, David Santillo, a senior scientist with the Greenpeace Research Laboratories at the University of Exeter, said these emissions are “very significant” and described the Environment Agency’s slow action as a “travesty”.

“The Environment Agency should be there to prevent this kind of thing, not just to document it and request more and more reports,” he said.

The EA said Huntsman “failed to act proactively” but it also “recognised that further follow-up sooner could have supported more timely implementation”. It added that its recent interventions have led to “significantly improved performance of the abatement system on site”.

Ally Lewis, professor of atmospheric chemistry at the University of York, said benzene is one of the most harmful air pollutants to human health and that the EA “seems to be allowing an obvious degradation in air quality and an increase in a pollutant that causes cancer on the basis that it’s fine as long as you stay below a somewhat arbitrary value”.

“If this is our national approach to managing risk and chemicals it seems remarkably laissez-faire and hands off,” he said.

Roel Vermeulen, professor of environmental epidemiology and exposome science at Utrecht University, said the modelling report flags a plausible problem that should be taken “very seriously”.

He said measurements of the benzene levels outside people’s homes and in other places in the community should “begin immediately” and this should be in parallel with reducing emissions.

A spokesperson from Huntsman said its own air monitoring data “indicates that concentrations beyond the site boundary are below applicable air quality standards”. It also said its “long-term personal monitoring programme highlights that there are no real-world instances of exceedance of exposure limits for personnel on site.” The company refused to share this data with the Guardian and has not shared it with the EA.

Campaigners say the benzene emissions from this factory point to a broader problem with the global plastic industry. A recent Greenpeace report said pollution from plastic waste is only one aspect of the “devastating impacts of plastics”, with the hazardous chemicals used in plastic production also “poisoning people and the natural world”.

International research has linked living close to plastic production facilities with negative health outcomes. The Boston College Global Observatory found that plastic production workers are at increased risk of a range of cancers, including leukaemia.

“You can’t manufacture plastics without creating pollution and the plastics then create pollution of their own. It’s a messy business right the way through,” Santillo said.

Carole Zagrovic, who worked as a community development specialist in Redcar for Friends of the Earth for around a decade in the early 2000s, said back then people in the area “talked about cancer like it’s the flu. They had become blase and hardened towards it,” she said.

Zagrovic said she was “appalled” that pollution like this was ongoing and said it seemed like nothing had changed despite her years of campaigning.

A spokesperson for Huntsman said: “Huntsman’s benzene emissions are fully compliant with our permit conditions, including our 2024 emissions, as governed by the Environment Agency.”

An EA spokesperson said: “We have been carrying out extensive regulatory work in response to concerns about emissions from this site, including inspections and compliance reporting which uncovered several breaches. We are considering further enforcement action in relation to these breaches and are working with the operator to ensure site improvements are rapidly delivered, due to our action, controls have been improved and emissions associated with process vent gases have reduced significantly since early February.”

title: What Ben Carroll’s cabinet cuts say about his ‘new direction’ for Victoria
excerpt:
A week after his elevation to premier and four months out from an election, the priorities of the Carroll government are becoming clearer

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get o...
body_text:
A week after his elevation to premier and four months out from an election, the priorities of the Carroll government are becoming clearer

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

It’s been exactly one week since Ben Carroll became Victorian premier, promising to differentiate himself from his predecessors Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews. With his new cabinet sworn in at Government House on Tuesday morning, Victorians are beginning to see what that actually looks like.

This was far more than tinkering at the edges. Four months out from an election, Carroll has made cuts and completely overhauled portfolios, and in turn, the priorities of his government.

“This is a strong, focused, united team that is taking our government in a new direction. A government that will fight every day for working people. A government that will fix things,” he told reporters.

The most striking feature of the new cabinet is which portfolios Carroll chose to abolish. Gone are the standalone transport infrastructure and Suburban Rail Loop portfolios that symbolised the Allan and Andrews governments’ focus. Carroll also scrapped the cost of living and the men and boys portfolios, the latter a national-first role established only four months ago by Allan to address the influence of the manosphere.

Carroll argues ministers responsible for health, roads and public transport should oversee infrastructure within their own portfolios, that “every” portfolio should be focused on easing cost-of-living pressures and his deputy, Gabrielle Williams, will take on responsibilities for gender equality. He also says removing the standalone portfolio does not necessarily signal the SRL’s demise – though he continues to dodge questions around a review into the costly project.

“This is a sign that we’re going to do things better, more efficiently and more effectively,” Carroll says.

– Leader of the Government in the Council

– Deputy Leader of the Government in Council

– Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy

Carroll has also slimmed the cabinet, confirming on Monday that the two vacancies created by the resignations of Allan supporters Lily D’Ambrosio and Harriet Shing will remain unfilled. He said on Monday it was a “simple measure” that showed he was treating taxpayers’ dollars with respect: the basic salary payable to an MP is $219,391 a year, while ministers receive an extra $184,407 and $19,628 in expense allowances.

Most Labor MPs agree its a politically smart move. But fiscally, the savings are modest. With Victoria’s debt forecast to approach $200bn over the forward estimates, the roughly $400,000 saved annually in ministerial salary allowances barely makes a dent.

The move also quietly strengthens Carroll’s position inside cabinet. A smaller cabinet reduces the influence of the Socialist Left faction while increasing the proportion of ministers aligned with the new premier.

Personnel decisions reinforce the same theme.

The biggest is Colin Brooks’ elevation to treasurer. Brooks is said to have built a reputation among business groups as industry and advanced manufacturing minister for being pragmatic and willing to engage with industry.

He also inherits industrial relations, placing him at the centre of ongoing pay disputes – including with school teachers and public hospital doctors.

Williams becomes the new education minister, who said she would contact the teachers’ union “as soon as I’m away from these microphones” in an effort to avert a third strike later this month. As deputy, she was able to chose her own portfolios.

Paul Edbrooke is another clear winner. Elevated to cabinet only in April, he now takes on the high-profile police, emergency services and crime prevention portfolios.

It’s telling both Edbrooke – a former firefighter – and Brooks – a qualified electrician who says he “grew up in a small business household” – emphasised their careers outside politics during Tuesday’s media appearance. As Labor seeks to reconnect with working-class voters considering backing One Nation, it will need more plain-speaking politicians front and centre. And Edbrooke’s addition of multicultural affairs also gives him responsibility to counter Pauline Hanson and One Nation’s rhetoric.

There were also losers. Several ministers associated with Allan lost influence. Steve Dimopoulos retains sport but loses major events and jobs. Paul Hamer gains roads but relinquishes corrections, youth justice and local government.

Symes – who was Victoria’s first female treasurer and was also seen as close to Allan – gained energy and environment – portfolios that will place her at the forefront of Victoria’s renewable energy transition and the politically fraught rollout of new transmission lines across regional communities.

Sonya Kilkenny is the only senior minister loyal to Allan who retained her major portfolios, after signing a deal last week to secure her positions as planning minister and attorney general in exchange for stepping down as a leadership candidate against Carroll.

The former police minister Anthony Carbines, one of Carroll’s closest allies, shifts into a new space, becoming the inaugural minister for AI and digital economy, as well as medical research, trade and investment and economic development. Other ministers who also broke ranks to support a leadership change were also rewarded, including Ingrid Stitt who takes on health and Enver Erdogan, who adds finance, government services, and keeps casino, gaming and liquor regulation.

Cabinet met on Tuesday afternoon, where the terms of reference for Carroll’s promised royal commission into the construction industry was expected to be discussed. What they look like will be the new premier’s first test.

After that, voters will be looking for more than rhetoric. They’ll want evidence that the change Carroll promises is real.

title: Bodycam video shows firefighters battling blaze in Spokane, US
excerpt:
Bodycam video shows firefighters battling blaze in Spokane, US

Bodycam footage from firefighters shows the speed needed to put out the blaze sweeping through the northwestern US. More than 60,000 peo...
body_text:
Bodycam video shows firefighters battling blaze in Spokane, US

Bodycam footage from firefighters shows the speed needed to put out the blaze sweeping through the northwestern US. More than 60,000 people have fled their homes as wildfires raged near Spokane, Washington for a third straight day.

title: France wildfires reveal hundreds of WW2 shells in village
excerpt:

A forest fire in the south of France has revealed a cache of 400 historic shells and m...
body_text:
A mother and son inspect the surrounds of their home in Le Porge on Monday, after it was destroyed in a wildfire

A forest fire in the south of France has revealed a cache of 400 historic shells and munitions in the village of Le Porge, according to local authorities.

Blasts, initially thought to be exploding gas cylinders, may have been World War Two explosives detonated by the heat of the fires, the local fire commander told local media.

More than 100 explosions were heard on the second night of the fire, Mayor Martial Zaninetti told French news outlet France Info, likening it to "the sound of war".

Demining operations have now seen most residents return to their homes, however the mayor has said certain areas are still off-limits. More than 180 houses in the area were destroyed by the wildfire.

"There were ammunition depots buried in land within our municipality, but we didn't know it, and they exploded", Zaninetti told France Info.

He described them going "to the right, to the left" and that there was "even one that went through a house".

A drone view of buildings destroyed by a wildfire in Le Porge

In a statement on Instagram on Monday, the mayor wrote that access to the ocean, a campsite, and the village of La Jenny remained off limits.

The historic weapons were both German and French and included mortar shells and anti-tank shells, French media reported.

Their discovery comes after a forest fire ravaged the Gironde area, which has now been brought under control after burning for about 10 days.

Pictures from Le Porge on Monday showed families picking through the burned remains of their homes.

On Monday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu thanked firefighters for their efforts saying "France has stood firm in the face of an unprecedented crisis".

He highlighted the battle against the fires had entered a "new phase" in the Gironde region, saying "the evacuated individuals are gradually returning to their homes".

Wildfires have raged across Europe over the two weeks, primarily in France and Spain, where more than 330,000 people were evacuated.

France was one of the worst affected regions, with an area of 42,000 hectares burnt in the south-west, making it one of the largest forest fires since World War Two.
