title: Teenager didn’t tell anyone Alan Jones allegedly kissed and touched him as he feared losing financial help, trial hears
excerpt:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

Alan Jones trial day one – as it happened

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A ...
body_text:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

Alan Jones trial day one – as it happened

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former schoolboy athlete has told the Alan Jones trial he didn’t tell anyone the broadcaster was allegedly kissing him and touching his genitalia when he was a teenager because he was “fearful” of losing Jones’s financial support.

The man, known as Complainant J, alleged that after he drove Jones to a function in Canberra and they were alone in the hotel room, Jones kissed him in a “smothering” way. After the drive back to Sydney, Jones allegedly said to him: “You’ve been a really good boy. I’m going to give you some more money.” His regular weekly stipend increased by $100, the court heard. J also said Jones told him he didn’t have to tell anyone he was giving him money as it was “a gift”.

The complainant said Jones always introduced him to people as being from “No 1 Struggle Street”, and he didn’t mind that.

The court heard the 2GB broadcaster befriended him when he was 14 after he broke an athletics record, and he went on to give the son of a single mother from the western suburbs a mobile phone, a car and up to $600 a week.

“I come from a small family, we struggled our whole lives, and I was getting everything handed to me, it was a wonderful life,” the man, who is now in his 40s, told day one of the Jones hearing.

“I thought if I told someone what was happening, I would lose everything.”

J said Jones first contacted him through his coach and invited him to visit him on multiple occasions and at first he had no idea who Jones was.

J told the court he caught the train to Circular Quay and visited Jones at his Macquarie Street apartment and they went out for a Chinese meal. After the meal, while they were watching tennis, Jones allegedly made comments about the size of an athlete’s penis. Jones said one sprinter had “a big cock”.

J said he took the “strange comment” as his cue to leave Jones’s apartment.

Jones gave him a hug and said “I love you mate”, J said. He told the court he replied with words to the effect of: “I love you too, you’ve done a lot for me.”

J alleged that Jones put his arm out for a “cuddle”.

“He pulled me slightly towards him and gave me a peck kiss on the lips,” the complainant told the court.

Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked J: “Did you consent to being kissed on the mouth that night?”

He replied: “No, I wasn’t given the opportunity.”

J said the kiss lasted for “half a second” and afterwards Jones’s “demeanour changed immediately” from “passionate I love you” to “business mode”. “I walked out and got the train home,” he said.

J at the time had a girlfriend and had discussed that with Jones, the court was told.

Throughout his testimony J tried to explain his conflicted relationship with Jones, and why he didn’t report the alleged indecent assaults at the time.

“I was fearful of him, but I was also accepting these things from him,” J said. “And I didn’t want to lose those things.

“The friendship I would say was tainted by the things that were going on.

Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or they distorted the truth.

Jones’s defence barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, earlier argued the alleged victims in the case were egged on to complain by media rivals and their reliability and credibility were questionable.

This included, Bashir alleged, shockjock Ray Hadley and Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons.

Bashir alleged FitzSimons harboured an intense dislike of Jones and encouraged complainants to make complaints about Jones.

Bashir also alleged that FitzSimons passed information to the Sydney Morning Herald’s investigative reporter Kate McClymont.

“This story sold newspapers,” Bashir said. “Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case.”

J was the first of six complainants who were expected to give evidence of their alleged indecent assault by Jones, who is facing 22 charges. The trial at Downing Centre local court was expected to run for four months and hear from 76 witnesses.

The judge, Glenn Walsh, was expected to hear from the six men who the prosecution will argue were significantly younger when they were allegedly indecently assaulted by the now 85-year-old Jones between 2003 and 2020.

title: Weather tracker: Austria breaks heat records as Japan braces for Typhoon Dolphin
excerpt:
Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges

Unbearable, record-breaking heat has dominated the summer of 2026 across much of Europe. Ne...
body_text:
Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges

Unbearable, record-breaking heat has dominated the summer of 2026 across much of Europe. New records were set in central Europe last week, with Wieselburg in Austria registering a new July peak of 40.3C (104.5F). This is particularly significant as it is just 0.2C behind the all-time high, set in the August of 2003.

However, not all of the northern hemisphere has experienced extreme heat and aridity. Vancouver recorded its wettest July since 2016 and the third wettest since 2008, with 33.6mm of rain. While that total may not appear exceptional, it is only a touch above the 1991-2020 climate average, highlighting how unusually dry July has been in the Canadian city over the past decade.

Meanwhile, Typhoon Dolphin has continued to barrel westwards across the Pacific Ocean towards Japan and Taiwan. It became the fifth category 5 tropical cyclone of 2026 and ranks third for wind speed, behind only typhoons Bavi and Sinlaku.

Dolphin reached maximum sustained wind speeds of 175mph on Thursday, with a central pressure of 910mb. The storm intensified rapidly over just 36 hours. On 27 July, it was a tropical storm, however, exceptionally warm sea temperatures of about 30C fuelled its swift transformation into a super typhoon. Another contributing factor was its unusually compact structure, with hurricane-force winds extending only 52 miles from the centre. By comparison, a powerful typhoon such as Dolphin would typically have a hurricane-force wind radius of about 100 miles.

As of Monday, Dolphin has been downgraded to a category 3 storm, with sustained wind speeds of 125mph. As it continues westwards towards the island of Okinawa, it is forecast to weaken further and make landfall as a category 1 or 2 typhoon.

However, wind speeds of 80-100mph are still expected to affect the archipelago and remain strong enough to cause widespread damage and disruption.

Although the overall wind speed of Dolphin is decreasing, its wind field is forecast to expand as it approaches land, shifting the primary threat from destructive winds to storm surge.

title: Central and southern Europe brace for heatwave – Europe live
excerpt:
Temperatures forecast to reach 37C in Budapest and Vienna as Hungary switches off vital nuclear plant with falling water levels in Danube affecting cooling capabilities

The latest heatwave seen in we...
body_text:
Temperatures forecast to reach 37C in Budapest and Vienna as Hungary switches off vital nuclear plant with falling water levels in Danube affecting cooling capabilities

The latest heatwave seen in western Europe last week are now moving eastwards, with large parts of central and southern Europe set to experience extreme temperatures near 40C, and putting countries at risk of an energy crunch.

Hungary was forced to shut down most of its sole nuclear power plant, which generates a large part of the country’s energy supply, for the first time in 44 years as the drying out of the Danube made it impossible to cool safely. The nuclear plant ‌is expected to ​be completely powered down later ⁠this week ​as water ​levels ​on ​the ‌Danube ​river are projected ​to fall further.

On Monday, many digital advertising screens will be turned off to save energy, as part of a broader push to seek savings wherever possible.

Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar warned on Monday that “the hardest five days are ahead.”

Romania and Serbia also reported their lowest-ever water levels, causing issues with hydropower generation.

Budapest and Vienna will see temperatures of up to 37C today, with Zagreb at 36C, Tirana at 35C, and Bucharest at 33C, and these temperatures are expected to last for up to five days.

But that doesn’t mean it will be necessarily much cooler in the west, with 36C in Rome and 34C in Paris.

Elsewhere, I will keep an eye on the political fallout from the migration crisis in Ceuta last week, with EU ambassadors meeting this morning for what is likely to be a fierce discussion on what’s next ahead of tomorrow’s talks between interior ministers.

I will bring you all the updates from across Europe as the day progresses.

It’s Monday, 3 August 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Record low water levels in Europe’s major rivers have curtailed the transport of goods, reduced electricity output and shrunk company earnings, stoking fears about the economic impact of searing heat and erratic rainfall, Reuters reported.

From the ⁠bustling port of Rotterdam to hydropower ​plants in Serbia, waterways have become a less reliable way to transport goods such as grains and oil, or to produce much-needed electricity when millions are seeking to cool their homes.

“It’s affecting not one region like we’ve seen in the past, but the whole ⁠European landscape,” said Alessandro Armenia, a power analyst at commodities data and analytics firm Kpler.

“Given the current dynamics, it means either we’re going to see blackouts or we need to invest way more.”

At Djerdap 1, Serbia’s largest hydropower plant, output has fallen to 20% of capacity, the plant’s production ‌director Davor Maljoković told Reuters, as the once broad shipping channel beside it has shrunk to expose sandbanks and gravel bars.

The lack of water has also disrupted cooling systems at Serbia’s Kostolac coal-fired power plants, forcing them to cut output, Serbia’s state EPS power utility said.

Romania’s state nuclear power producer Nuclearelectrica also had to shut one of its two reactors earlier this week for the same reason, with the second expected to soon follow.

Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens on Sunday, killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified.

Footage showed one of the helicopters losing control in the face of gale-force winds that have pushed flames towards settlements on Athens’ western fringes.

“The pilots … were taken unconscious to hospital, where their death was confirmed,” said the fire department’s director of communications, Vassilis Vathrakogiannis.

The Greek prime minister, Kyriakos Mitsotakis, said the two dead were a Dane and a Greek. The two crew members of the second helicopter were rescued.

title: Trump suggests new talks with Iran to begin on Monday
excerpt:
"I think there's a deal" - Trump on calling off Iran strikes

US President Donald Trump has said new talks with Iran will begin on Monday, after calling off what he said would have been "massive" stri...
body_text:
"I think there's a deal" - Trump on calling off Iran strikes

US President Donald Trump has said new talks with Iran will begin on Monday, after calling off what he said would have been "massive" strikes on the country.

"They knew the extent of the attack because they saw it forming," he told reporters on board Air Force One on Sunday. "We're talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon."

In an earlier post on Truth Social, Trump said he had been asked by Iran and US allies in the Middle East to "hold off" on any attack as the "perimeters" of a deal had been agreed.

Iran's foreign ministry said there are no plans to receive a US delegation or send Iranian's to Washington. Earlier talks have been facilitated through mediators.

The US president has repeatedly vowed that a negotiated end to the war is near, only for tit-for-tat strikes to resume.

In his remarks on Air Force One, Trump declined to outline a deadline for a deal to be struck with Tehran, adding: "We'll just see how it is. We're ready to go anytime we want... I'm not looking to kill people."

Trump added that Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman - as well as US partners such as the United Arab Emirates and Qatar - had urged him against conducting strikes over the weekend.

"We were all set to go," Trump said. "The reason they asked is [that] they think there's a deal," he said. "There's a deal on Hormuz, and there will be a deal on the nuclear."

Global oil prices fell on Monday morning in Asia trading after Trump's announcement. Brent Crude oil was down by 4.5% at $83.98 (£62.26), while US-traded oil was 4.6% lower at $80.74 (£59.85).

Energy prices have fluctuated since the conflict started on 28 February as traders reacted to disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Around 20% of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) usually flows through the strait.

Iran's semi-official Mehr news agency denied that Tehran had asked the US to hold off on further military action, saying Trump's claims were "nothing but a new lie".

On Sunday, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said that negotiations with Oman on a deal on the Strait of Hormuz were "on track for finalisation", according to Iranian media.

The US president has not yet made clear the venue for the talks on Monday, nor the potential attendees.

During his remarks on Air Force One, Trump said that the planned strikes would have been "the biggest attack since World War II", and could have derailed prospects of a negotiated end to the months-long war.

Trump declined to answer if he had been planning to strike Iranian energy infrastructure, which international law experts have said could constitute a war crime.

Iran's acting Defence Minister Majid Ibn al-Reza earlier said Tehran viewed every threat from its adversaries as "real and credible" even if it formed part of psychological warfare.

"We will neither be caught off guard nor remain passive," he added.

The US president has previously issued apocalyptic warnings to Tehran, only to subsequently insist that diplomacy was being given a chance.

In his post on Saturday, he said the US was "locked and loaded and ready to go against the Islamic Republic of Iran, at levels of Military Terror, Strength, and Power not seen since World War II".

But he added cancelling the attack would be "for the future benefit of the world and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran".

Back on 7 April, the US president warned that "a whole civilisation will die tonight" if Iran refused to engage in peace talks. At the time, he also threatened to destroy civilian infrastructure and power plants.

That threat did result in historic face-to-face talks in Pakistan, led by Vice-President JD Vance. However, those negotiations did not result in a deal.

The Trump administration has also been largely dismissive of data showing the war - and its economic impact - are broadly unpopular with Americans, including with many Republicans.

Polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the handling of the war have prompted alarm among some conservative strategists ahead of the coming November midterms.

With additional reporting from Peter Hoskins.

title: Greens senator brands Pauline Hanson a ‘political coward’ over press conference bans – as it happened
excerpt:
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has rubbished Pauline Hanson’s decision to bar the Guardian, the Age and the ABC from a One Nation press conference today.

Hanson-Young claimed Hanson was “running s...
body_text:
Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has rubbished Pauline Hanson’s decision to bar the Guardian, the Age and the ABC from a One Nation press conference today.

Hanson-Young claimed Hanson was “running scared of scrutiny”, calling her “a politician who thinks that she should have the right to say whatever she wants, but no one else should have the right to ask questions”.

“Pauline Hanson is showing herself to be a political coward by hiding from certain media because she doesn’t like questions from journalists, and this is a very very bad start to any political campaign,” the Greens senator told a press conference in Parliament House this afternoon.

As we reported earlier, reporters from the ABC, the Age and the Guardian were not provided with the time or location of the press conference to announce One Nation’s Victorian state election candidates.

“I’m not putting up with the spin, gotcha moments, wanting to have a go at me … [and] treat us totally different to what you do the other major political parties. Enough is enough,” Hanson said of her decision at the press conference.

That’s where we’ll leave our live news coverage.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

The government has released new details of its news bargaining incentive legislation, after consultations with industry.

The high-profile trial of former broadcaster Alan Jones for indecent assault and sexual touching charges began today in Sydney’s Downing Centre local court and is expected to run for four months and hear from 76 witnesses.

Laurie Daley has ended months of speculation by officially quitting his role as NSW State of Origin coach.

A Senate inquiry into the Albanese government’s gambling laws has heard allegations that betting companies and casinos are providing big spending punters with drugs, free accommodation and escorts.

Tolls are set to fall on some Sydney motorways after the operator Transurban reached a long-awaited deal with the NSW government.

Pauline Hanson held a press conference in Melbourne where reporters from the ABC, the Age and the Guardian were barred from attending.

Two people are being treated for leg and neck injuries after a partial collapse of a seven-metre-high building in inner Sydney, according to Fire and Rescue NSW.

Tests by the CSIRO have confirmed Australia’s first mass mortality event from the deadly H5 bird flu and the environment minister, Murray Watt, has warned more mass wildlife deaths will occur as the disease continues to spread. There has also been a suspected H5 bird flu mortality event in Victoria.

Thanks for joining us, see you tomorrow morning!

A mining site in New South Wales’s Hunter Vally has paused operations after a worker died on Monday after “a mobile equipment incident”.

The death happened at the United Wambo Open Cut mine, about 16 km west of Singleton, owned by mining companies Glencore and Peabody.

Glencore said emergency services and police are onsite, and mining operations have been suspended.

In a statement, CEO of Glencore’s Australian operations Peter Sharpe said:

double quotation markOur sincere condolences go out to the worker’s family, friends and colleagues. This is tragic news for our entire workforce. Our immediate focus is on providing support to the worker’s family and our employees.

In a statement, NSW Minerals Council CEO Stephen Galilee said:

double quotation markThis tragedy highlights the hazards faced by those working in our industry and is a sombre reminder of why the safety of our workforce must always be our number one priority.

Former ACCC chair has ‘real concern’ over news bargaining scheme

The former competition watchdog boss Rod Sims says the government has a “lack of ambition” on the news bargaining incentive, raising concerns that many smaller publishers will miss out on deals and that not enough money will be raised from the big tech companies.

Sims, a former chair of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, said there were positives in Labor’s latest plan, including making progress on the framework after it had appeared stalled, and changes to include LinkedIn – which had previously been carved out from the plan that includes TikTok, Google and Meta platforms.

But Sims says the government should be looking to raise higher sums than it has outlined.

The assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino said today that the NBI “should see benefit to the media in the order of $200 million to $250 million” – but Sims said that was similar to what the former news bargaining code raised five years ago from only two companies at the time (Google and Facebook).

Sims said the government should be aiming higher than that, more in the realm of $300m plus, with more companies included and inflation added.

double quotation markThere’s a lack of ambition, and simple arithmetic here.

Sims also worried that many outlets would miss out on benefit, with big tech companies only obligated to make six deals minimum. He said.

double quotation markIt just means not everybody will get a deal, in fact most won’t … some outlets in public interest journalism won’t get some. That’s a real concern.

Another former ACCC chair, Alan Fels, gave similar feedback. He said it was positive the government was making progress, but worried the scheme didn’t go far enough to “extract more from the platforms” for Australian journalism.

A Microsoft spokesperson, responding to the inclusion of their service LinkedIn in the NBI, said the company “shares the Government’s objective of promoting a sustainable Australian news ecosystem” and said it would continue “constructive engagement with Government, publishers and industry stakeholders to support high-quality journalism, innovation and economic growth.”

Little penguins among species at risk from H5 bird flu, says Victorian biodiversity chief

In an update on Victoria’s H5 bird flu situation, the state’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said the little penguins at Phillip Island and St Kilda were among the species considered at risk from the deadly virus.

He said the state government was working with Phillip Island Nature Park and Zoos Victoria on the potential for vaccination in little penguins and in captive threatened species held by Zoos Victoria.

double quotation markObviously one of the challenges around vaccines is that you need to be able to administer more than one dose, that’s largely impractical for wild populations. But we’re working with Phillip Island Nature Park in relation to penguins and also Zoos Victoria in relation to a range of threatened species.

The state’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said aerial and ground surveillance in the south-west of the state – around Portland and Nelson – showed “clear evolution of a form of cluster that is entirely consistent with what has happened in South Australia”.

double quotation markLast week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change as the disease spreads out and has further impacts.

Aerial surveillance in the south-west since 14 July showed a “clear increase in the number of dead terns” along the coast, he said. However, access to some areas, such as Lawrence Rocks, was limited by large swells. The area is home to an important breeding colony of Australasian gannets, seal colonies as well as the Glenelg Estuary and Discovery Bay, an internationally significant wetland site.

South Australia’s environment minister says she is concerned about a confirmed case of H5 bird flu in a petrel found in the Coorong, one of several new locations where the deadly disease has been detected in the state.

The migratory petrel is one of 18 confirmed new cases in SA. The new cases include a silver gull in Glenelg, two greater crested terns at Troubridge Island, a silver gull at Southend, a greater crested tern at Monarto and six greater crested terns on Pages Islands.

Five greater crested terns and a silver gull at Baudin Rocks also returned positive results. Those birds were a sample from about 50 dead and 30 sick birds found by aerial surveillance at Baudin Rocks in what has been confirmed as Australia’s first H5 mass mortality event.

The Coorong is a large area that is home to internationally significant wetlands that support populations of waterbirds and migratory species.

SA environment minister Emily Bourke said:

double quotation markThat confirmed location is of concern because it is where waterbirds are also located.

So it’s going from seabirds, but also potentially now into where we know a lot of water birds are nesting and using this space as a safe haven.

Media freedom alliance condemns Pauline Hanson’s press conference bans

The Alliance for Journalists’ Freedom has condemned One Nation’s Pauline Hanson for barring the Guardian, the Age and the ABC from a press conference today.

Executive director Peter Greste said “no political party should have the right to pick and choose the news outlets who ask them questions”.

double quotation markOne of the strengths of our democracy is the ability of all journalists to robustly interrogate politicians on behalf of the people who hire them – the voters. It isn’t always comfortable, but that freedom is one of the reasons our political system is one of the world’s most stable and effective.

By locking out the ABC, The Age and The Guardian, One Nation is directly weakening our democratic system.

Two men sustain neck and leg injuries after building collapse in Sydney

Two people are being treated for leg and neck injuries after a partial collapse of a seven-metre-high building in inner Sydney, according to Fire and Rescue NSW (FRNSW).

FRNSW said emergency services responded to the incident around 11am on Wattle Street in Ultimo, where a total of seven people were assessed by paramedics.

Ambulance NSW say the two men, both in their 60s, were taken to Royal Prince Alfred hospital and St Vincent’s hospital, where they are now in stable conditions.

Earlier we incorrectly reported that one of the men was in his 30s.

FRNSW said the wall collapsed on to an adjoining service station, where debris damaged several parked cars.

The service station remains closed as a precaution, and its employees have been evacuated. Some neighbouring buildings have also been cleared.

News Corp claims media bargaining changes ‘gut’ scheme

The government’s changes to the News Bargaining Incentive have also not impressed News Corp, with the publisher claiming the updates would harm Australian media outlets.

News Corp’s Australian chair, Michael Miller, was unhappy with the changes to settings which would see narrow the charge base of how the fee is calculated on big tech companies, but increase the rate of charge. He said:

double quotation markThese changes gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media, right when those rules need strengthening, not softening.

On an already uneven playing field, getting this wrong won’t just hurt Australian media. It will erode the quality and independence of news every Australian relies on.

Tech giants cannot keep dodging their obligations. Australia deserves full revenue transparency, backed by severe, non-negotiable penalties for any platform that flouts local law.

News code changes will ‘short-change’ Australian media, Coalition says

The Coalition claims Australian journalists will be “dudded” by the government’s changes to the News Bargaining Incentive, and that the new framework will not collect enough money from big tech platforms.

Shadow communications minister Sarah Henderson and shadow assistant treasurer Kevin Hogan have released a statement on today’s announcement, calling it “a concerning free kick to the multinational tech giants at the expense of Australian news outlets” and raising concerns it would lead to “dramatically short-changing Australian media companies.” They said:

double quotation markWhile the government has increased the charge rate to 2.5 per cent, it is estimated this about-face will mean billions of dollars of revenues earned by the tech giants will not be included in the scheme.

Henderson accused Labor of letting big tech “off the hook” with the changes. She said:

double quotation markNot only will Labor’s scheme mean less money for Australian journalism, the government is now doing even less to encourage commercial deals with big tech which is extremely disappointing.

Labor’s dithering and delay on a promised replacement scheme has left tech giants unaccountable for their use of Australian copyrighted news content, while newsrooms and regional newspapers face uncertainty about their future.

Hogan said the Coalition welcomed the inclusion of LinkedIn in the scheme – which had previously been given a carveout under the draft framework.

NSW Icac hears of potentially illegal meetings between Reformers after summons

The NSW Icac has adjourned early for the rest of the day. Not long before lunch, Reformers witness Robert Assaf admitted to having three meetings with another person named in allegations, Jeremy Greenwood, after receiving a summons to appear at a private hearing before the inquiry this year.

Under section 114 of NSW’s Icac Act, it can be a criminal offence if a person discloses any information about a summons from the watchdog “that is likely to prejudice the investigation to which it relates”, punishable by up to 12 months imprisonment.

Asked about meetings at a cafe in Belfield and another on the Cooks river track in Sydney, Assaf admitted the men left their phones and laptops in Greenwood’s car before going for a walk so their conversations could not be traced.

Assaf said during the meetings they discussed the nature of evidence they would give to Icac, including potential vulnerabilities for the group at the inquiry.

Counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, asked: “Did you understand at that point in time, given what you were told when you received the summons, that it was important not to discuss your evidence?”

Assaf, who has described being stressed and nervous after receiving communication from Icac, admitted that he did.

The inquiry will return tomorrow with the NSW shadow attorney general, Damien Tudehope, and businessman Frits Maré expected to give evidence first.

That’s all for me. Achol Arok will take things from here, take care.

The theme of the 26th Garma festival was Bukmak, meaning all of us, everyone together in Yolngu language. The four-day gathering at the Gulkula ceremonial grounds in Arnhem Land is the largest First Nations cultural event in Australia.

The Victorian government said a cluster of dead and sick greater crested terns had been identified through aerial surveillance in the Glenelg River estuary near Nelson and across Lawrence Rocks over the weekend.

The government has not yet provided the number of birds observed but state authorities will speak to media later this afternoon.

Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer, James Todd, said the observations were consistent with what was recently reported in South Australia, where mass deaths of crested terns at Baudin Rocks were confirmed earlier today as Australia’s first mass mortality event from the deadly disease.

Victoria’s chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said investigations were under way to better understand the progression of the virus in wildlife.

double quotation markThis event is consistent with the type of wildlife impacts we have been preparing for as H5 bird flu becomes established in a bird population.

Sampling has taken place today, along with further aerial surveillance, to determine any further impacts in other species.

There have so far been seven confirmed positive H5 bird flu cases in Victoria in crested terns, five in Portland and two in Nelson.

Guardian Australia has released a statement after being barred from Pauline Hanson’s press conference earlier today.

As reported earlier, reporters from the ABC, the Age and the Guardian were not provided with the time or location of a press conference to announced One Nation’s Victorian state election candidates.

double quotation markHolding public figures to account is the role of a free press and an essential part of the democratic process. It is disappointing that One Nation continues to prevent the Guardian and other news outlets from reporting on its press conferences. Our journalists should be able to ask questions in the public interest and not be deterred from doing their job.

The Guardian has published important public interest journalism on Pauline Hanson and One Nation and stands by the rigour of its work.

title: AstraZeneca holds talks with Bristol Myers Squibb on $400bn merger
excerpt:
Tie-up would be one of the biggest-ever pharmaceutical deals and create the world’s fourth-largest drugmaker

Britain’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, is understood to be in discussions to take over ...
body_text:
Tie-up would be one of the biggest-ever pharmaceutical deals and create the world’s fourth-largest drugmaker

Britain’s biggest drugmaker, AstraZeneca, is understood to be in discussions to take over its US rival Bristol Myers Squibb in a deal that would create a near-$400bn (£300bn) pharmaceutical group.

AstraZeneca, run by Pascal Soriot, its longtime chief executive, is the second-biggest listed company in the UK, with a market value of nearly £196bn before the news broke. BMS, headquartered in Princeton and known for its cancer treatments, is worth $133bn.

A tie-up would be one of the biggest-ever pharmaceutical deals and create the world’s fourth-largest drugmaker by market value. The talks were first reported by the Financial Times.

AstraZeneca’s FTSE 100-listed shares plunged more than 7% to a low of £116.46 in early trading in London, as investors reacted to news of the talks. BMS’s shares rose 3.5% in pre-market trading in New York.

A deal would expand AstraZeneca’s presence in the US, where it is already investing $50bn in research and manufacturing by 2030. It completed a direct listing of its shares on the New York stock exchange in June, and a deal with BMS could revive fears of a shift away from the UK.

The news surprised analysts, who questioned the rationale behind a tie-up and noted that any deal would be closely scrutinised by regulators, given the overlap of the companies’ oncology portfolios.

Analysts at Jefferies, led by Michael Leuchten, said: “‘Why is perhaps not yet clear to us: we suspect that most people will focus on the potential to establish an even bigger oncology powerhouse, with the resultant portfolio likely the broadest in the industry. However, beyond the regulatory hurdles we would argue that pipeline assets could be sourced elsewhere, as AstraZeneca has been doing, particularly in China.”

Chris Beauchamp, a chief market analyst at the investment platform IG, said: “Though a rare example of a big UK firm buying a smaller US firm is something to warm the cockles of the British heart, it risks the departure of yet another national champion, and in any case the pair’s large cancer divisions is a major hurdle to a successful deal. BMS has struggled since 2023, and some Astra shareholders will wonder at the need to do expensive M&A when their shares are doing so well.”

While talks have been held in recent months, there is no certainty that a deal will be concluded, according to sources.

AstraZeneca, headquartered in Cambridge, was formed in 1999 from the merger of the Swedish company Astra AB and the UK company Zeneca Group. Zeneca had been spun off from Imperial Chemical Industries five years earlier.

AstraZeneca’s share price has more than quadrupled during Soriot’s leadership, when it overtook its UK rival GSK in size.

Under Soriot, the FTSE 100 company fended off a hostile bid from its US rival Pfizer in 2014 that valued AstraZeneca at almost £70bn. He then successfully rebuilt the company’s drug pipeline with cancer immmunotherapies – drugs that harness the body’s immune system to fight tumours – and other treatments.

A week ago, AstraZeneca said it was confident of hitting its growth targets for 2030, by which it expects to achieve $80bn (£60bn) in annual sales, up from $59bn last year, despite the surprise failure of Wainua, one of its leading heart disease drugs in development. Soriot said the company must move at “Chinese speed” to ensure it does not fall behind competitors.

A few days later, BMS beat Wall Street expectations with its second-quarter results and lifted its 2026 outlook. It made revenues of $12.97bn during the quarter, up 5% on a year earlier, excluding currency movements.

Its UK research team is based at Moreton on the Wirral peninsula near Liverpool, while its commercial head office for the UK and Ireland is in Uxbridge.

John Murphy, a senior pharma analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said a deal made “limited strategic sense” for AstraZeneca.

“Their growth outlooks are very different – double-digit earnings gains are forecast at Astra through 2030, with Bristol set for continued declines, due to multiple patent expiries – and, while both are focused on developing promising pipelines, history suggests such megamergers hamper pipeline progress,” he said.

“Major cost savings via eradication of overlapping infrastructure is one obvious benefit, but would suggest reduced confidence at Astra in its pipeline and growth outlook. A link-up in certain disease categories may be a possible area of future collaboration.”

AstraZeneca declined to comment. BMS has been contacted.

title: Jasprit Bumrah ruled out of Sri Lanka Test series due to injury
excerpt: India pace ‌spearhead Jasprit Bumrah has been ruled out of this ⁠month’s two-Test ⁠series against Sri Lanka as he continues to recover from a left knee injury, the country’s cricket ⁠board (BCCI) has ...
body_text:
India pace ‌spearhead Jasprit Bumrah has been ruled out of this ⁠month’s two-Test ⁠series against Sri Lanka as he continues to recover from a left knee injury, the country’s cricket ⁠board (BCCI) has said.

The BCCI on Monday named uncapped fast bowler Auqib Nabi as Bumrah’s replacement after the 32-year-old withdrew from the squad ‌due to persistent discomfort in his knee.

Bumrah, who sustained the injury while fielding in a one-day international against England in Cardiff in ⁠July, was initially included in the squad subject to a final fitness test and had been undergoing rehabilitation at the BCCI’s Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru.

Nabi, 29, who hails from Jammu and Kashmir, earned his first senior call-up after impressing in domestic cricket, taking 104 wickets across the last two Ranji Trophy seasons.

He took 60 ⁠wickets in the 2025-26 Ranji Trophy season ⁠to help his domestic team win their first title. He also featured for India A on their tour of Sri Lanka in June-July, claiming six wickets ⁠in two first-class matches.

Nabi is the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to receive ⁠a call-up to the senior Test ⁠side.

The BCCI added that batter Sai Sudharsan’s participation remains subject to fitness clearance.

The series begins in Galle on August 15, with the second Test scheduled in Colombo ‌from August 23.

Shubman Gill (captain), KL Rahul (vice captain), Yashasvi Jaiswal, Rishabh Pant (wicketkeeper), Sai Sudharsan, Dhruv Jurel (wk), Ravindra Jadeja, Kuldeep ‌Yadav, ‌Manav Suthar, Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna, Gurnoor Brar, Devdutt Padikkal, Saransh Jain and Auqib Nabi.

title: Two crew killed as British pilot survives after firefighting helicopters collide in Greece
excerpt:
Watch: Moment before helicopters collide while tackling Greece wildfires

Two crew members have been killed after two helicopters collided mid-air in Greece as they were battling wildfires, local auth...
body_text:
Watch: Moment before helicopters collide while tackling Greece wildfires

Two crew members have been killed after two helicopters collided mid-air in Greece as they were battling wildfires, local authorities say.

The fatalities were a Danish pilot and a Greek fire service liaison officer. A British pilot and another Greek co-ordinator on the second helicopter survived.

Video of the incident some 65 km (42 miles) west of the capital Athens shows one of the two Bell helicopters hitting the propellers of the other, which bursts into flames and crashes in a ravine. The other aircraft made an emergency landing.

Wildfires have broken out in Greece this week, prompting mass evacuations. Other European states have also suffered devastating blazes during prolonged heatwaves.

According to the Greek Fire Service, the two leased Bell helicopters collided on Sunday while taking part in efforts to tackle a large wildfire burning on the Attica-Boeotia border.

The crew members of one aircraft were rescued alive, while the second crew were recovered unconscious and later pronounced dead.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed his "deepest sorrow" over the accident.

In a post on X, he said the loss of the Greek coordinator and Danish pilot "fills us all with grief". He also sent condolences to their families.

Firefighters and forensic experts were later seen working at the crash site

According to protocol, all Bell helicopters across the country have been grounded, a source from the civil protection ministry told the BBC.

The source added that the second Bell helicopter involved in the collision made an emergency landing in an area of low vegetation.

"The two people on board, a British pilot and a Greek fire service liaison officer - escaped with minor injuries," the source said.

"Both remained conscious and have been admitted to hospital, where they will remain under observation for 24 hours as a precaution."

The source also told the BBC the British survivor was a private pilot hired for the wildfire season.

He was not part of any exchange between the UK and Greece, and there was no request for assistance from Athens.

Meanwhile, Greece's Ekathimerini news website said the two survivors immediately reported the collision, guiding rescuers to the crash site.

The names of the four crew members have not been publicly released.

Erickson Air-Crane and Chinook helicopters, as well as Canadair water-bombing aircraft are continuing to carry out firefighting efforts.

Early this week, France and Spain battled huge fires - two of the main ones were close to Madrid and Bordeaux respectively. Those have now been contained, though they are still burning. Some 300,000 people who were evacuated have started to return to their homes.

In Greece, media reports describe "a titanic battle" along a swathe of territory that includes Porto Germeno, Psatha, Fokida, Megara and Kefalonia, where more than 500 firefighters have been struggling to bring the situation under control over the past 72 hours.

Most wildfires are sparked by people, whether intentionally or accidentally, but climate change is making the conditions for them more common.

Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive hot spells, generating fuel for wildfires.

title: Hero sheepdog becomes unlikely rescue partner after unexpected move aids first responders
excerpt:
A sheepdog jumped into action herding a field full of goats out of the way so first responders could safely touch down in Laguna Beach, California.

A Southern California sheepdog is being hailed as a...
body_text:
A sheepdog jumped into action herding a field full of goats out of the way so first responders could safely touch down in Laguna Beach, California.

A Southern California sheepdog is being hailed as an honorary first responder after police drone video captured the hardworking pup helping clear the way for an emergency helicopter.

The Laguna Beach Police Department shared drone video Friday showing officers and firefighters responding to an emergency in the city's foothills as crews prepared a landing zone for a helicopter.

As crews worked on the ground, a hardworking white sheepdog sprang into action, herding a nearby group of goats away from the landing area and helping keep the helicopter's path clear.

Drone video released by the department shows the dog weaving behind the herd as dozens of goats move up the hillside and away from the helicopter's approach.

FBI, ATLANTA POLICE TARGET UNAUTHORIZED DRONES FLYING NEAR WORLD CUP VENUES

A herd of goats moves across a hillside as an emergency helicopter approaches during a Laguna Beach rescue response. (Laguna Beach Police Department)

At one point, the camera zooms in on the pup happily trotting across the hillside with its tail wagging after completing its impromptu mission.

"The sheepdog stepped up and helped guide a group of goats out of the way so the units could work," the Laguna Beach Police Department wrote in a social media post. "That's a good boy."

Officials have not publicly released details about the emergency response or what prompted the helicopter deployment.

CRUISE PASSENGER HAILED AS HERO AFTER JUMPING INTO WATER TO SAVE 84-YEAR-OLD MAN

Southern California sheepdog earned praise as an honorary first responder after drone video showed it herding goats away from a helicopter landing zone during an emergency response in Laguna Beach. (iStock)

The feel-good video quickly won over social media, where viewers crowned the four-legged helper "Sgt. Sheepdog" and praised the pup for calmly guiding the herd of goats out of the way.

DOG SAVED FROM ISIS BY ARMY VETERAN 'KIDNAPPED' FROM FAMILY YARD BY LOCAL AUTHORITIES

A Laguna Beach Police Department patrol SUV parked along a street in Laguna Beach, California. (Laguna Beach Police Department)

The Laguna Beach Police Department appeared to agree, writing simply, "That's a good boy."

Fox News Digital reached out to the Laguna Beach Police Department and the Laguna Beach Fire Department for additional information about the emergency response, including what prompted the helicopter deployment and for comment.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Ms Rachel claims 'no one needs a billion dollars,' endorses Democratic progressives Abdul El-Sayed, Cori Bush
excerpt: Hosts on 'Fox & Friends' discuss far-left activists' anti-ICE protests at facilities like Delaney Hall in Newark, N.J., where nearly 100 people were arrested. YouTuber Ms. Rachel, popular for children...
body_text:
Hosts on 'Fox & Friends' discuss far-left activists' anti-ICE protests at facilities like Delaney Hall in Newark, N.J., where nearly 100 people were arrested. YouTuber Ms. Rachel, popular for children's content, is shown leading sing-alongs with kids at the facility, raising questions about politicalization.

Popular children's YouTube educator Ms. Rachel backed a dozen progressive Democratic candidates on Friday, including former Rep. Cori Bush, D-Mo., and Michigan U.S. Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed, using her audience of more than five million followers to promote candidates she believed cared about children.

"I think all kids and people should have medical care. I don’t think anyone needs a billion dollars ever, I think all kids should be safe from violence," Accurso said in a post on Instagram.

Accurso's slate covered House and Senate contests in eight states. It also included Vermont Rep. Becca Balint, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon and former Tennessee state Rep. Justin Pearson.

YOUTUBE STAR MS RACHEL GIVES FUNDS TO DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED

Ms. Rachel endorsed Cori Bush, Abdul El-Sayed and 10 other progressive candidates, telling her five million Instagram followers she backs those who protect kids. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images)

"These are the folks I believe care about all kids," Accurso said.

Bush, who is seeking to reclaim her former St. Louis-area seat from Rep. Wesley Bell in Tuesday’s Democratic primary, is a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member. In early July, Bush said in a post on X that she was proud to be re-endorsed by the DSA.

"Together, we’ll work to abolish ICE, deliver Medicare for all, end wars overseas, and achieve true economic justice," Bush said.

EX-'SQUAD' MEMBER FIGHTS FOR COMEBACK AS SOCIALIST WING RAMPS UP WAR ON DEM ESTABLISHMENT

Children’s educator Rachel Griffin Accurso, has more than 20 million YouTube subscribers. (Maxine Wallace/The Washington Post via Getty Images)

El-Sayed rejected the socialist label during a Tuesday interview with MS NOW host Jen Psaki despite him receiving endorsements from Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, D-N.Y., El-Sayed spoke at six DSA events between 2017 and 2020.

"I’m simply not a socialist ... I've studied a lot of the solutions that I fight for," El-Sayed said to Psaki. "Things like Medicare-for-all, things like rethinking the way that our financial system implies that corporate CEOs are more interested in a quarterly bottom line than they are in the long-term sustainability of their business."

El-Sayed’s campaign platform calls for Medicare-for-all, taxing billionaire wealth and banning corporate money in politics.

A federal filing also listed a $3,000 payment from Accurso to his campaign ahead of Tuesday’s Michigan primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. The filing did not specify whether the payment was a contribution or a loan.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

In her post, Ms. Rachel said that politicians "shouldn’t attack each other." (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)

Accurso also connected her endorsements to the influx of what she described as outside money in Democratic primaries.

"I think politicians shouldn’t attack each other and I don’t think big groups should be able to use millions to attack candidates," Accurso said.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) previously criticized Accurso's financial support for El-Sayed, whose platform calls for an arms embargo against Israel.

NRSC spokeswoman Samantha Cantrell addressed the two in a statement to the New York Post in July.

"Abdul El-Sayed and Ms. Rachel are one and the same, forcing their socialist, they/them, anti-America agenda on our children," Cantrell said.

Ms Rachel also recently weighed in on the investigation into Nolan Wells’ mysterious death, with a now-viral social media post pointing to unsupported allegations that race played a role in law enforcement’s handling of the case. (Nathan Congleton/NBC via Getty Images; Christine Wonsley/Facebook)

Accurso has increasingly used her platform, which includes a YouTube channel with more than 20 million subscribers, for political advocacy.

In June, Accurso visited Delaney Hall, an immigration detention facility in Newark, New Jersey, and traveled to Washington to urge Congress to end family detention and separation.

Accurso said on Wednesday that she is involved with politics because she cares "so much about kids and families everywhere," and said she could not watch them suffer and "not stand with them" in an Instagram post where she simultaneously endorsed El-Sayed.

Fox News Digital reached out to Accurso, Bush, the DSA and El-Sayed for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

title: Entire Squad endorses Abdul El-Sayed days before Michigan Democratic Senate primary
excerpt: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said during an interview that he was "simply not a socialist" when pressed on his association with prominent left-wing leaders such as Bernie Sanders and Rep. ...
body_text:
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said during an interview that he was "simply not a socialist" when pressed on his association with prominent left-wing leaders such as Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

Every member of the "Squad," an informal left-wing congressional caucus, has endorsed Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, according to his campaign website.

The Squad is made up of Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Ayanna Pressley, D-Mass., Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., Summer Lee, D-Pa., Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and Greg Casar, D-Texas.

Many of the squad’s current and former members have past or ongoing affiliations with the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization El-Sayed is attempting to distance himself from as he attempts to moderate ahead of a swing-state general election.

The unified endorsements sharpen the ideological stakes of the Tuesday primary, linking El-Sayed to the party’s most prominent progressive bloc even as he rejects the socialist label and seeks to present himself as a viable candidate in a battleground state. The support also gives Republicans an early line of attack should El-Sayed defeat the more centrist Stevens and advance to the general election.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., is among the members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

DEM PRIMARY ERUPTS AS ESTABLISHMENT FAVORITE DISMISSES RIVAL AS ‘CELEBRITY CANDIDATE’

"The entire Squad has now endorsed Abdul El-Sayed to carry on its radical, socialist, anti-American agenda in the U.S. Senate, and they will be rejected by Michiganders at the ballot box," National Republican Senatorial Committee regional press secretary Samantha Cantrell told Fox News Digital.

Casar was the most recent Squad member to endorse El-Sayed, throwing his support behind him Thursday.

"Abdul El-Sayed is showing what it means to run a bold, pro-working class campaign," Casar said. "House progressives need strong partners in the Senate in order to put money in your pocket, get money out of politics, and win Medicare for All. I’m proud to endorse Abdul."

SOCIALIST-BACKED DEM WHO RIPPED THE WEALTHY CRACKS STATE’S TOP 1%, TAX RETURNS SHOW

Every member of the "Squad," an informal left-wing congressional caucus, has endorsed Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

Casar, Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib and Lee all have current or former Democratic Socialists of America affiliations. El-Sayed at one point even appeared at a Democratic Socialists of America event alongside Tlaib.

El-Sayed headlined that event, a fundraiser that brought in roughly $10,000 for the Detroit Democratic Socialists of America, and was photographed next to Tlaib behind a table with a poster on it depicting a hand labeled "DSA" choking a snake labeled "capitalism."

The Michigan Senate hopeful attended and spoke at six Democratic Socialists of America events between 2017 and 2020, Fox News Digital previously reported. Organizers affiliated with the socialist organization have described El-Sayed as "a longtime friend of Detroit DSA."

ABDUL EL-SAYED SAYS RALLYING WITH HASAN PIKER DOESN'T MEAN HE ENDORSES 'AMERICA DESERVED 9/11' REMARK

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders join hands following a campaign rally on July 18, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Jose Juarez)

Despite pulling in endorsements from socialists and his longtime association with the Democratic Socialists of America, El-Sayed rejects the socialist label and has distanced himself from the group.

"I'm not technically or practically DSA," El-Sayed told The Wall Street Journal in early July.

In an interview with CNN, he said, "I am not somebody who is a socialist. I believe in capitalism, I just believe that capitalism has to be regulated."

El-Sayed faces off against Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary Tuesday. Stevens is widely viewed as the more centrist of the two. Polls generally show El-Sayed leading Stevens by a comfortable margin, according to the New York Times.

The El-Sayed campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
